title: Port Moresby at 'unnecessary risk' as landholders block urgent water works
text:
Urgent repairs to address a pending water crisis in Papua New Guinea's capital have been delayed after traditional landowners set up a blockade, restricting access to a leaking pipeline that supplies more than half the city's water.

Engineering reports seen by the ABC say the raw water pipeline is in "active failure" and has a powerful leak ejecting 10 million litres of water every day.

If the pipe bursts, Port Moresby would instantly lose more than half its water supply, creating a health and security emergency for the city's 1 million residents, the reports said.

Port Moresby's water supply network facing 'imminent failure' A decades-old pipeline supplying water to nearly 1 million people in Papua New Guinea's capital is at risk of collapsing without urgent repairs, documents reveal.

Work to repair the leak was scheduled for this weekend after months of detailed planning involving foreign governments, including Australia, and the United Nations.

But the company this week announced the repairs would be delayed after traditional landowners set up a blockade, preventing access to the site of the leak.

The damaged section of pipeline is located on the outskirts of Port Moresby on customary land owned by the Behori Clan.

Members of the Behori Clan seen assisting during previous PNG Water works. (Supplied: Behori Clan)

"This blockade is creating great uncertainty and throws all preparations for a shutdown into limbo," Water PNG board chairman Meckles Poya said.

He said it put the city at "unnecessary risk" and threatened Port Moresby residents' right to access water and sanitation.

"We are all in this together and people around the capital city are preparing and supporting Water PNG to get in and fix this problem," he said.

Traditional owners calling for compensation

Foxie Kaeaka, who represents the Behori Clan that set up the blockade, said landowners wanted compensation for access to the site and were also seeking reparation for ancestral remains unearthed during Water PNG works at a different site in 2024.

"They have to fairly and adequately compensate the Behori clan for that," Mr Kaeaka said.

Foxie Kaeaka says the Behori Clan has been cooperating with Water PNG, but wants outstanding issues addressed. (ABC News: Marian Faa)

Documents seen by the ABC show Water PNG paid $1,600 to the clan to conduct burial rituals at the time and a further $5,000 for archaeologists to excavate the site.

Water PNG said the landowners were demanding a further $1.6 million in compensation, but Mr Kaeaka said they were open to negotiation with authorities and had not settled on a figure.

He said the Behori Clan had maintained a close and cooperative relationship with Water PNG over many years and had helped originally identify the leaking pipeline.

Ancestral remains were unearthed on Behori Clan land during Water PNG works in 2024. (Supplied: Behori Clan)

"We are not saying 'no' to the repair. All along we have been cooperating with Water PNG," Mr Kaeaka said.

"All we are saying, all we are demonstrating, is that we have an issue and you haven't attended to us."

Port Moresby 'at needless additional risk'

Water PNG said it wanted a peaceful resolution to the dispute but could exercise powers under PNG law to access the site without landowners' permission.

"The National Water Supply and Sanitation Act is clear that Water PNG has full authority to access the pipeline," Mr Poya said.

"Water PNG has undertaken meticulous planning and already delayed the repairs so that additional equipment and expertise can be brought in to ensure the success of the repair work, but this blockade is now placing Port Moresby at needless additional risk."

The site of a major pipeline leak on the outskirts of Port Moresby. (ABC News: Marian Faa)

Ahead of the scheduled emergency repairs, Australia had provided technical expertise and specialised equipment had been urgently transported from Australia, China and the Netherlands.

Water availability was expected to dramatically reduce while repairs took place over three days, with water rationing schedules in place across the city.

Elective surgeries had been put on hold, hotel bookings had been limited and police were gearing up to manage the outage, Water PNG said in a statement.

Last month, the ABC revealed the leaking pipeline was just one in a series of major water issues facing Port Moresby due to decades of underinvestment in infrastructure maintenance and upgrades.

"Port Moresby's water supply system is now operating under extreme and unsustainable risk, with multiple critical assets … at or beyond end-of-life," a Water PNG report from November 2025 states.

"These critical assets have suffered protracted degradation and are showing signs of imminent failure."

The Behori Clan is seeking reparation for ancestral remains unearthed during Water PNG works at a different site in 2024. (Supplied: Behori Clan)

The report warned the city's water system had almost no redundancy or storage buffer and a major failure was likely to rapidly reduce water supply to the city with cascading health, security and economic consequences.

Major repairs and upgrades to the city's water infrastructure were likely to cost around $700 million, the report estimated.

It also said Water PNG was effectively insolvent, with the PNG government owing more than $80 million in unpaid water bills to the cash-strapped utility.

title: K-pop powerhouse BTS say they will not submit music for 2027 Grammys
text:
K-pop powerhouse BTS say they will not submit their music for consideration at the forthcoming 2027 Grammy Awards.

All seven BTS members — RM, Suga, j-hope, Jimin, V, Jung Kook and Jin — shared a coordinated message announcing the news.

"We hope our music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language," it read.

"We thank Army and everyone who has always stood by us."

Wednesday's announcement came just over a month after the Recording Academy — the organisation that hosts the Grammy Awards — introduced five new categories.

Among the newly created categories is an award for the best Asian pop music performances, which some fans claim is a racialised barrier for Asian performers.

A representative for BTS offered no additional comment.

BTS has never won a Grammy, though they have been nominated for five: three times in the best pop duo/group performance category as well as album of the year (for their contributions to Coldplay's Music of the Spheres) and best music video for Yet to Come.

In fact, no K-pop act had ever won a Grammy before this year, when Golden from the Netflix animated film KPop Demon Hunters took home the trophy for best song for visual media. It capped a highly visible night for K-pop at the Grammys — an institution where the genre has long been under-celebrated despite its massive international following.

Korean pop band says they will not n give their music for consideration at the forthcoming 2027 Grammy Awards, file photo. (AP)

In March, BTS returned after a nearly four-year musical hiatus.

ARIRANG, the 14-track, critically acclaimed fifth studio album from the septet, served as both a reintroduction to the band after its members completed South Korea's mandatory military service and as a keen reminder of their place atop popular culture conversation.

Representatives for the Recording Academy did not immediately respond to The Associated Press' request for comment.

title: Test that could identify Alzheimer's signs 20 years earlier greenlit for trials
text:
The ability to test for signs of Alzheimer's disease decades earlier could be a step closer with a new blood test set for clinical trials within months.

Laboratory test "pTau217" is thought to give results in as little as 18 minutes and can detect changes in the brain decades before someone might develop symptoms.

It works by detecting a protein called phosphorylated tau 217 which is a biomarker for a build up of amyloid plaque in the brain.

This sticky plaque is thought to play a central role in Alzheimer’s disease.

The Therapeutic Goods Administration has approved the pTau217 test which researchers announced at the launch of the Asia-Pacific Centre of Excellence for Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis in Sydney.

The centre is a collaboration between medical research group Neuroscience Research Australia (NeuRA) and pharmaceutical company Roche aims to enable earlier and more accurate detection through advanced blood-based biomarker testing.

According to the Alzheimer's Association, the disease is the most common form of dementia in Australia.

It affects memory, thinking and behaviour, with symptoms developing enough to interfere with daily tasks, the association says.

NeuRA said it would "alleviate the burden of delayed and uncertain diagnosis" for Alzheimer's.

A spokesperson said the rollout for doctors to refer patients was expected in the next six to nine months.

Alzheimer's advocate Louise Bryant spoke about the difficulties her partner had getting a diagnosis. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

Alzheimer's advocate Louise Bryant said the announcement of a potential blood test to detect the disease early was deeply personal.

She said her partner, affectionately known as Moose, was diagnosed with early onset dementia at just 46 years old.

"He was first diagnosed with what was believed to be alcoholic-related dementia." Ms Bryant said.

"But the following 10 years his behaviour shifted repeatedly and then there were concerns perhaps his dementia might carry a genetic risk."

Ms Bryant said it was only in the two months before he died that it was officially confirmed through an invasive lumbar puncture that he had Alzheimer's.

"That result would not have changed the outcome, but an earlier diagnosis would have removed some of the stigma and the uncertainty," she said.

"Perhaps it would have given us earlier access to some other treatment options."

'A new frontier for Alzheimer's care'

NeuRA chief executive Professor Matthew Kiernan said the blood test had been approved for clinical trials.

"Having regulatory approval of these blood tests is a new frontier for Alzheimer's care," Professor Kiernan said.

Professor Kiernan has welcomed the development. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

The body said the new centre addressed a critical gap for tackling the disease in Australia and Asia-Pacific.

"The Centre of Excellence will enable earlier and more accurate Alzheimer's detection through advanced blood-based and spinal fluid biomarker testing, positioning NSW as a national hub for dementia diagnostics, clinical trials and research innovation," a NeuRA spokesperson said.

Roche Diagnostics Australia general manager Anand Vairavan said Alzheimer's diagnosis was "currently extremely slow and complex" and undertaken with "expensive imaging and invasive lumbar punctures".

"It's about the gift of time," Mr Vairavan said.

Federal Health Minister Mark Butler said there had been an "almost structural delay in people getting an effective diagnosis of the different forms of dementia".

"Finding a blood test for biomarkers is a holy grail for this disease," Mr Butler said.

"It will be a huge advance in this enormous challenge we have."

PM hails 'massive breakthrough'

Dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, accounted for over 17,500 deaths in 2024, and was now the nation's leading cause of death, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

NeuRA said the human, social and economic toll of dementia was immense, with "annual costs already surpassing $4.7 billion" and increased pressure on clinicians and the health system.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says the announcement "provides hope". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told ABC News Breakfast the announcement was a "massive breakthrough".

"It's really important and provides hope at a time where I think the world needs more hope and less fear as we go forward," Mr Albanese said.

Mr Albanese said the disease was a tragedy that affected many families.

"I lost a good friend of mine — he passed away on Monday, Chris Raper, who was a union official at the Miscellaneous Workers Union, and a dear friend.

"He was severely affected, as so many Australians are by dementia."

title: Teacher used laptop decorated with a 'free Palestine' sticker, inquiry told
text:
Students at a New South Wales public school competed to be crowned "king of the Jews" in a game they created to trip up their Jewish peers, the royal commission on antisemitism has heard.

Antisemitism in schools and against young people has been a key focus of the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion.

The inquiry on Thursday heard from NSW Board of Jewish Education (BJE) CEO John Hamey.

Mr Hamey said parents of Jewish-Australian students often reported instances of antisemitism to the BJE, with one incident involving a game called "trip the Jew" being played at a NSW public school.

He said students would score points if the Jewish student fell, and whoever had the most points at the end of the day was "crowned the king of the Jews".

Mr Hamey, who is Catholic and not Jewish, spoke of another incident where he observed a teacher at a NSW public school using a laptop decorated with a "free Palestine" sticker which included a crossed-out image of the Israeli flag and Star of David.

"They said to me that they were proud to be anti-Israeli," he said.

Mr Hamey, who was the principal of Jewish day school Moriah College from 2011 to 2018, said he told the teacher they were "creating a hostile environment for students that were Jewish in that classroom context".

"She was not fulfilling her responsibility to be non-partisan and apolitical in the classroom," he said.

Mr Hamey said there must be "better systems to respond to hate speech" in schools.

"There needs to be a clear reporting of instances of antisemitism and hate speech in schools, and that can take place within existing frameworks," he said.

"There needs to be a much more formalised system so we understand the degree and extent and reach of antisemitism in our public schools."

title: Cricketer dubbed 'Clicky Ponting' suspended as stats show unusual trend
text:
The club at the centre of the "Clicky Ponting" scandal in English amateur cricket has suspended its player over the matter.

Saltburn Cricket Club said Brian Devine had been suspended for the rest of the season after several videos were posted online with claims Devine was clicking his fingers as the ball passed the bat to mimic the sound of an edge.

The club has forfeited its next match in the North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League.

"We are treating this allegation with the utmost seriousness and, as a family-centric club, we are fully cooperating with the league's investigation," a statement read.

"We believe that the club acted decisively as soon as the complaint and investigation were made known to us.

"The player at the centre of the complaint has been suspended and will not play again for the club this season or in the foreseeable future, pending the outcome of this investigation."

Devine is yet to comment on the matter and an investigation into the claims has yet to be completed, with the allegations so far unproven.

However, an amateur data analyst on social media platform X said they had trawled all scorecards from Saltburn games, and found wicketkeeper catches dramatically increased when Devine was playing.

"Been requested to split it by the matches where Devine (the slip clicker) played, and it's even more stark," X account @maxtempers, which usually posts about British politics, wrote.

"39 keeper catches in 13 matches with Devine. 5 keeper catches in 7 without."

The post followed an original analysis that found wicketkeeper catches increased four-fold when the keeper involved in the alleged clicking footage was playing, including eight catches in one innings.

The record at Test level is seven catches in one innings, shared by five players.

"The League has received a formal complaint regarding alleged incidents in a Division Two game on Saturday 25 July, 2026," a league statement read when the controversy came to light

"A full investigation has been initiated and until such time as the formal processes are complete, no further comment will be made."

Australian cricket podcasters The Grade Cricketer have offered to provide financial support to Devine and Saltburn.

title: Portrait of Alex Ryvchin wins Archie People's Choice
text:
Michael Zavros has won the People's Choice Award for the 2026 Archibald Prize for a portrait of author and Jewish advocate Alex Ryvchin.

Accepting the award, worth $5,000, Zavros said the acknowledgement of visitors to the Archibald Prize was "genuinely humbling".

"I'm deeply grateful that this portrait has connected with so many people."

In his artist statement, Zavros said he had seen Ryvchin — the co-CEO of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry — in the media a lot after October 7, 2023 terrorist attacks by Hamas on Israel.

"He spoke passionately about the pain in his community and the changes he feared would emerge in our nation," Zavros wrote.

The artist, who recently uncovered his own Jewish heritage, then saw Ryvchin in the media again after December's Bondi attack.

"I found common ground with this man who, like me, is a father of three," Zavros wrote in his artist statement. (Supplied: AGNSW/Jenni Carter)

In his acceptance speech, Zavros said "Alex again showed the kind of leadership that many Australians were searching for" in the wake of the attack.

"Overwhelmingly, I don't believe Australians are racist. I don't believe we are homophobic and I don't believe we are anti-Semitic. Those things have no place in the country we aspire to be," Zavros said.

Zavros also spoke about the common ground he shared with Ryvchin, being the child of migrants from Cyprus in the 50s, while Ryvchin was four when he and his family migrated to Australia from Ukraine as refugees in the 80s.

"What unites us is so much more powerful that was divides us, though it's easier to focus on the latter," he said.

"I'm immensely proud of this work that Alex and I have made together."

A portrait of outspoken advocate Ryvchin winning the Archibald People's Choice comes as the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion continues this week.

Zavros took out the audience-voted prize after a record 45,769 visitors voted.

Zavros's win follows Richard Lewer winning the $100,000 Archibald Prize in May, for his portrait of Pitjantjatjara elder, artist and ngangkari (traditional healer) Iluwanti Ken. In April, Sean Layh won the Packing Room Prize, for his portrait of actor Jacob Collins in character as Shakespeare's Hamlet.

Richard Lewer wins Archibald Prize Richard Lewer has won the $100,000 Archibald Prize for his portrait of Pitjantjatjara elder Iluwanti Ken.

Zavros is one of 59 finalists in this year's Archibald, alongside portraits of Bondi hero Ahmed Al Ahmed, Governor-General Sam Mostyn and former ABC journalist Virginia Trioli.

Past winners of the People's Choice Award,first awarded in 1988, include Loribelle Spirovski for her finger-painted portrait of musician William Barton (2026), Angus McDonald for his portrait of academic Marcia Langton (2024), and Jaq Grantford for her portrait of actor Noni Hazlehurst (2023).

The importance of symbols

Zavros's hyper-realist oil painting of Ryvchin, which stretches to more than 2 metres tall, was staged at a secluded Sydney bay suggested by Ryvchin.

In his artist statement, Zavros explained he always knew he wanted to paint Ryvchin in "water, or 'the sea'".

"[It] symbolises so much for Jewish and non-Jewish Australians alike," he wrote.

He also decided to include his tefillin — small black leather boxes with leather straps that contain scrolls inscribed with verses from the Torah.

" Symbols are so important in contemporary culture. All too often, when marking identity, they are used to harm people. "

He added in his speech symbols like the tefillin "express faith, history and belonging, yet too often they are used to divide and to harm".

Presenting the award to Zavros, AGNSW director Maud Page said she had noticed how visitors would "pause in front of this beautiful poignant work".

"There's no doubt that Alex Ryvchin's incredibly sad eyes and stance alone on the shoreline has propelled people to think a little bit more about their own mortality and beliefs."

She also praised Zavros's "immaculate brushstrokes".

"He works with assuredness, able to not only render a subject in his total likeness, but also position him within an evocative narrative setting, where the very ripples of water on the sand convey as much as the twist of Alex's body," she said.

"The painting, for me, is a picture of 2026."

The Archibald, Wynne and Sulman Prizes 2026 exhibition runs until August 16 at the Art Gallery of New South Wales.

title: Kavinsky, French producer behind Drive hit Nightcall, found dead at home
text:
French electronic musician Kavinsky, best known for his haunting track Nightcall, made famous by the 2011 movie Drive and performed at the 2024 Paris Olympics, has died aged 50.

The producer, real name Vincent Belorgey, was discovered dead at his Paris home on Tuesday evening, the Paris prosecutor's office said.

Parisian authorities have opened an investigation into the cause of death but first responders found "no suspicious elements" at Belorgey's home, the prosecutor's office stated.

Part of the rich French electronic music scene spearheaded by Daft Punk and spawning 2000s contemporaries like Justice and SebastiAn, Kavinsky was hailed as one of the country's "most singular voices" in a tribute from Culture Minister Catherine Pégard.

"Both danceable and nostalgic, his music will continue to resonate across generations and borders," the minister wrote in a post on X.

French President Emmanuel Macron also paid tribute on Facebook, calling the musician "forever a source of French pride".

Born in the Parisian suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis in 1975, Belorgey originally pursued acting before his music career took off in the mid-00s.

Drawing inspiration from 16-bit video games, 80s film soundtracks and a love of luxury cars, he developed a synth-heavy take on French house music.

In 2006, under the pseudonym Kavinsky, Belorgey released his debut EP Teddy Boy, made entirely on a vintage Yamaha DX7. It featured Testarossa Autodrive, a single that helped develop the "synthwave" sound and coincided with the wider "blog house" and "electroclash" scenes of the 2000s.

The 1986 EP followed in 2007 and Kavinsky went on tour with Justice, SebastiAn, and Daft Punk, including the latter's Nevereverland tour of Australia, featuring The Presets and Cut Copy.

His anticipated 2013 full-length debut album OutRun (sharing its name with Sega's classic 1986 arcade racing game) reached the second spot on the French album charts.

Double J — a place for music lovers Double J gives you the new music you'll actually love, alongside the classic tracks you keep coming back to. Give your playlist a rest and join us here.

The record also developed Belorgey's Kavinsky alter ego: In the 80s, a young man crashes his Ferrari Testarossa and returns as a zombie in 2006 to make electronic music and haunt highways in sunglasses and fast cars.

That persona inspired his 2010 song Nightcall, which achieved mainstream success for its use in Drive, Nicolas Winding Refn's 2011 thriller starring Ryan Gosling as a former stuntman-turned getaway driver.

Co-produced with Daft Punk's Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo, the nocturnal tune balances stalking synth with a romantic chorus featuring singer Lovefoxxx from Brazilian band CSS. It has been streamed more than a billion times combined across Spotify and YouTube.

Kavinsky explained the song was about an unrequited romance between his zombie alter-ego and a past girlfriend who had moved on with "a new boyfriend and kids," he explained in a 2011 interview.

" He's melancholic [and] has some regrets and now he's trying to be a good man but he can't because he's dead. "

Kavinsky's 2022 album Reborn, a 2024 re-release of Nightcall featuring French indie rock band Phoenix and Belgian artist Angèle, coincided with Kavinsky performing the track at the Paris Olympics closing ceremony. This version reached number three in the French charts.

Loading Instagram content

The Weeknd called Kavinsky an "inspiration" and news of his death "heartbreaking" on social media.

The Canadian pop sensation collaborated with the French producer on 2016's Odd Look, which was a hit in France in 2013, originally featuring SebastiAn.

Fellow French DJ David Guetta called him "a true icon of French electronic music" on Instagram.

title: Regional council hands maternal and child health service to state government
text:
When Jes Matthews became a mother, her maternal and child health nurse became a lifeline.

"She's like a family member. She's like an aunt, really," Ms Matthews said.

"I don't think I'd have the confidence to know my son was actually OK [without her]."

Living in Bendigo away from family, Ms Matthews relied on regular visits for breastfeeding support, weight checks and reassurance that her five-month-old son Bill was thriving.

The City of Greater Bendigo has announced plans to hand the maternal and child health service (MCH) back to the Victorian government.

Ms Matthews fears future parents may not receive the same "critical" support.

"It just seems like a shock … it might really throw people," Ms Matthews said.

"If it's not based quite so much in the community, it might be difficult to have mums' groups and connections to other services that the council offers for babies and young parents.

"I don't know. It just feels difficult."

Jes Matthews says she has relied on regular maternal and child health nurse visits. (Supplied: Jes Matthews)

Bendigo council has decided to step away from funding the MCH service by the end of the year, with the transition to a new provider expected before the end of 2026.

Chief executive Andrew Cooney said the decision was about ensuring the service was best placed to support families into the future, rather than simply being about funding.

"We think for the next stage of this service delivery, better service can be provided through the health system," he said.

Mr Cooney said maternal and child health nurses were increasingly supporting families with more complex needs, and moving the service into the public health system could provide better access to coordinated care, clinical support and career opportunities for nurses.

"There's much better support and much better career progression for a nurse in a public system than there is in the council," he said.

"We know the community really values being able to visit a service in their community, and that's going to be pretty important for us as we work through the transition."

Funding shortfall

The City of Greater Bendigo is one of several Victorian councils, alongside Loddon Shire, Campaspe Shire and Hepburn Shire, transitioning responsibility for the MCH service away from local government.

Andrew Cooney says the decision is not just about funding. (Supplied: City of Greater Bendigo)

The service has operated in Victoria for more than 100 years and has long been described as an "international gold standard" by the Municipal Association of Victoria (MAV).

In 2022, the MAV signed a memorandum of understanding with the Victorian government recognising councils and the state as equal funding partners.

But a 2024 Victorian parliamentary inquiry found councils believed state funding had failed to keep pace with rising costs.

Swan Hill Rural City Council Mayor Stuart King told the inquiry councils were effectively covering about 70 per cent of the cost.

The Victorian government rejected that assessment, saying it did not agree the funding model was insufficient.

Jennifer Anderson says councils are facing growing financial pressure. (Supplied: Jennifer Anderson)

MAV president Jennifer Anderson said councils across the state were facing growing financial pressure.

"We've been saying for some time that this level of funding has been dropping off and the costs to staff and everything else involved with the service has increased over time, yet the funding hasn't," she said.

An analysis of Loddon Shire's budgets over the past decade found state funding increased, but at a slower rate than wages, insurance and operating costs.

Last year, the Victorian government invested $202 million in maternal, child health and early parenting centres across the state.

But Ms Anderson said that funding did not restore the former cost-sharing arrangement.

"It sounds like a lot of money, but it's certainly not covering that 50-50 cost sharing that councils have been doing in the past," she said

Weakening community connections

Victorian Association of Maternal and Child Health Nurses president Catina Adams said moving the service into the public health system risked weakening the community connections that underpinned it.

"It doesn't belong in the public health system … it runs the risk of diluting the service," she said.

"We nurses home-visited over 80,000 families within two weeks of their arrival home.

"It's just such an important connection, which, if [replaced with] a nurse within a public hospital system, I think would be completely lost."

Federal Health Minister Mark Butler said child and maternal health services across the country need to be "bolstered".

He said the new Thriving Kids program would provide nurse support for children under nine with developmental delay and/or autism, using a mix of new and existing services, including MCH nurses.

Mr Butler said he was less concerned about whether services sat with councils or the state, as long as families continued to receive support.

"I'm a little agnostic about whether they're delivered through state systems or council systems … we just want to make sure it's there," he said.

title: Number of children in residential care in Qld jumps to record new highs
text:
Almost 3,000 children were in residential care (resi-care) in Queensland in March, a new record high, and a stark increase from the more than 2,200 recorded in the previous year.

There was also an increase in children under five in the system, putting further pressure on the state government's vow to remove them.

The shocking data was released in conjunction with the government's response to the commission of inquiry into child safety.

The 11-month inquiry found no child had been adopted from state care since 2019, making 52 recommendations to shift the focus to family-based care.

Following the report's release in June, Minister Amanda Camm committed that all children under five years old would be removed from residential care.

Minister Amanda Camm "committed to Queenslanders" that the number of children in residential care would go down. (ABC News)

The latest data showed 107 children under five were in resi-care in March, up from 78 the previous year.

Ms Camm said the peak of 2,819 children in residential care recorded under her tenure would be exactly that.

"I will be marked on that," she said.

"That is the line in the sand, and that is my message to Queenslanders, and it's also why we have embarked upon an ambitious recruitment process for foster and kinship carers across this state."

The government has accepted in full 32 of the 52 total recommendations from the report. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

Response times to respond to urgent child safety matters went backwards on every metric compared to the previous year.

More than 10 per cent of matters requiring a response in 24 hours were not commenced in that time frame.

Just over 4 per cent of matters requiring a response in a week met that benchmark.

Child safety officers were, on average, supporting almost 16 children each.

"I am confident that my department has worked diligently to ensure that they make the assessments appropriate, but is there room for improvement? Yes, there is," Ms Camm said.

Support for young people and families The Butterfly Foundation: National helpline 1800 ED HOPE (1800 33 4673), 8am-midnight (AEST/AEDT), 7 days a week

ReachOut Australia: Confidential online peer support for young people and online resources for wellbeing

Headspace: Centres in each state and territory or check out eheadspace for online support

The Kids Helpline: 24-hour support on 1800 55 1800

Lifeline: 24-hour support for all Australians on 13 11 14

'The work starts today'

The government accepted 32 of Commissioner Paul Anastassiou KC's recommendations and accepted in principle 16.

Attorney-General Deb Frecklington said the response centred around five key areas.

"The best interests of the child are paramount," she said.

"Strengthening early intervention and prevention, improving stable and permanent care arrangements, streamlining child litigation and the role of the courts, and updating the legislative framework through staged reforms to better protect vulnerable children.

"The system was and is broken, so the work starts today."

Queensland's Attorney-General Deb Frecklington said the government wouldn't be sitting on its hands. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The government has budgeted $200 million this financial year to implement the changes.

Key accepted recommendations include a feasibility status to assess the concept of simple adoption, and to entrench adoption as an option regardless of cultural background.

That previously drew criticism from First Nations advocates, who claimed there was no way to separate adoption from the history of the Stolen Generation.

But several key accepted or accepted in principle reforms recommended to be implemented in 12 months will take two and a half years to roll out.

Those included reforming when a child can be removed from their family, prioritising family contact as part of child protection orders, and improving child protection officer case management.

Ms Frecklington said the government wasn't "going to sit on our hands".

"There is a way forward here with the time frame, and there is also massive legislative change required to take place to ensure that, first and foremost, the paramount principle is the best interest of the child."

The government and Ms Camm have come under fire recently, following reports of children in care sleeping on the floor of child safety offices.

Department redesign recommended

A full restructure and redesign of the department of child safety was recommended, but the government only accepted that in-principle.

Ms Camm noted she had sacked several high-level bureaucrats and was driving accountability.

"We will also be looking very closely at our existing structure, what needs to change, our 20 per cent uplift in the front line, and how we can drive the resources where they need to be," she said.

The government has budgeted $200 million to implement the changes. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

"I will hold my Director General and the Department to account, and Queenslanders will hold me to account."

Two inquiry recommendations were listed for "further consideration".

The first was replacing "custody" and "guardianship" with "parental responsibility", with the commissioner noting the two former words failed to recognise the nuance of care arrangements.

The second was that financial assistance was given to any person granted care of a child.

The government said each would be "further considered as part of a subsequent tranche of more complex legislative reform".

A further two recommendations were "noted", including that the government ensure legal representation for all parties in a child protection proceeding.

The government highlighted the assistance provided by Legal Aid Queensland in child protection matters.

title: Farmers seek solution to mounting plastic waste problem
text:
Rows of black and white plastic weed mats line Jodi and Phill Brown's paddocks where tomato, chilli and capsicum seedlings are getting their best start in life.

Hidden underneath, black trickle tape slowly delivers water and fertiliser directly to plant roots, while the blanket above prevents weeds and shields the soil from the north Queensland sun.

"We've had a lot of issues with trying to get rid of plastic, a lot of farms have got big piles, you can see them," Ms Brown says.

At the end of the immaculate planting rows the refuse of seasons past is piled as high as Ms Brown is tall.

"Back in the day it all got picked up and taken out to the rifle range and used as a backing to shoot into," Mr Brown said.

"But they don't need it anymore, they've got enough," Ms Brown said.

Plastic weed mat prevents weeds from taking over fruit and vegetable paddocks in north Queensland. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

Waste piles up

An essential tool for modern horticulture, farmers remove the plastic after harvest and roll it into bundles to be collected and dumped in landfill, which can cost thousands of dollars.

Others looking to avoid the costs have illegally burned or buried it.

At the Brown's Bowen farm, 200 kilometres south of Townsville, the loss of a reliable, affordable collection service has meant truckloads of used plastic are piling up.

Phil Brown has been growing fruit and vegetable crops in Bowen for more than 20 years. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

"The businesses are so busy that you can't get anybody to dump it, so even if you could afford it, there's nobody who can transport it," Ms Brown said.

"We're just going to have to get rid of it in dribs and drabs, a truckload at a time."

Agricultural waste consultant Anne-Maree Boland said the Brown's experience was not isolated.

"We know that there's at least 100,000 tonnes of plastics per annum that are produced on farm and a large proportion, probably two thirds, is in the horticulture sector," she said.

"We have estimated about 7 per cent of the total amount that is recycled."

Farmers lay trickle tape to irrigate and fertilise paddocks in the horticulture industry. (Supplied: RMCG)

Ms Boland said the further farmers were from recycling infrastructure, the more expensive solutions became.

"If you're transporting [plastic] more than 300 kilometres, the costs start to outweigh the benefits," she said.

Grazier Sandra Richards spent time searching for an option to recycle the plastic waste, first for her cattle and forestry operation at Richmond in the state's north west, and after selling the farm, for the broader agricultural industry.

"I became interested in waste, which really led me to discover the very large problem that exists on farms," she said.

" Particularly in north Queensland, which is so far away from any capital city, there's nothing. "

Sandra Richards is hoping to find suitable land to build an agricultural waste recycling plant in north Queensland. (Supplied)

Ms Richards worked on a Townsville project hoping to turn recycled agricultural plastics and timber waste into composite products for use as railway sleepers and park benches.

Despite showing promise, it never got off the ground.

Mayor of the Whitsundays Ry Collins, who worked alongside growers in the Bowen Gumlu region before being elected, said even in one of Australia's key food bowls it was difficult to make the projects financially viable.

"If it's a commercial business that's ultimately hoping to turn a profit, they need to show it can stack up fairly quickly and stand on its own two feet," he said.

Cleaning the plastic is also a significant issue, one that can make or break a proposal.

Farmers invested in technology that is now defunct after a previous recycling project fell through in Townsville. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

The Browns invested about $30,000 to make a special tool to sweep their plastic matting clean in preparation for a recycling program.

"They said if you sweep it all properly and separate your plastic and your trickle tape, we'll take it," Mr Brown said.

But the program failed to get government funding and collapsed.

"That was frustrating," Mr Brown said.

Searching for a solution

Ms Richards is working with a family-owned Chinese recycling company to establish a new large-scale processing facility in Townsville.

"They've been over quite a number of times looking at availability of waste plastics, which is huge," she said.

Robert Ho said his family chose to partner with Ms Richards because the project was close to both the farmers and Asia.

Robert and Michael Ho are interested in establishing an agricultural waste recycling facility in north Queensland. (Supplied)

"In the past, we didn't have this [recycling] technology," he said.

"People thought, 'We can just throw it away, we can just export it,' but it's not going away.

China bans foreign rubbish China's ban on foreign waste is reverberating through Australia's waste industry, but local operators see it as a wake-up call.

"If you export and you bury the rubbish, it's not going away from the earth."

Their facility could wash and process about 20,000 tonnes of plastic collected directly from farms each year to be turned into agricultural products like produce bags.

But after several years of planning, a suitable site with the right combination of power, water and proximity to the Townsville Port has not been found.

The Queensland government last month released its Less Landfill, More Recycling 2035 strategy, which commits almost $1 billion over five years to improve recycling infrastructure across the state.

However, it does not specifically address agricultural plastic recycling.

Environment Minister Andrew Powell said there was a lack of investment in the farm plastics problem.

"If there's an innovator out there, a company or a council that want to team up with farmers to come up with a solution, we're ready to work with them," he said.

Ms Brown said she hoped a practical solution would arrive soon.

"It's a huge problem, we can't put it anywhere else, so it's just sitting there stockpiled," she said.

title: Woman faces legal action over video of driver in racist road rage incident
text:
Jessica Roberson has seen road rage before, but she was shocked when she witnessed a driver take his hands off the wheel to pull his eyes back in a racist gesture towards her ride-share driver.

The 38-year-old said her driver had slowed down in Gold Coast traffic as they approached a car accident, when the driver of a ute behind began honking his horn.

"He pulled up alongside us and did a racially charged gesture towards my Uber driver," she said.

Ms Roberson filmed the incident and said she felt obliged to apologise to her driver for the other driver's actions.

"I was absolutely mortified that anyone would do that to another person," she said.

"My Uber driver was more concerned about not aggravating him … she was like, 'It's OK, it's OK.'"

Ms Roberson's online response to the action she witnessed two weeks ago has led to legal threats and demands for a retraction by the driver's company.

Social media posts and legal threats

Ms Roberson said she was frustrated by the interaction and shared it to social media to push for the company to take "accountability" for the driver's actions.

With no way of identifying the driver, she instead highlighted the fact the vehicle in the footage belonged to hydro vacuum excavation company Provac Australia.

Jessica Roberson posted the video of the incident to her social media page. (Supplied: Jessica Roberson)

Ms Roberson began her first video with the words: "TikTok, you need to do your thing and find this fruit loop because I am so sick of racist pigs."

Her videos quickly gained traction and received hundreds of thousands of views before the company responded with a cease-and-desist letter three days later.

The 10-page document, seen by the ABC, states the company has suffered commercial harm because of Ms Roberson's videos and asked that she remove them immediately.

"You have sought to attribute the conduct of one individual employee to Provac as a company and have conveyed, encouraged and perpetuated the false imputation that Provac itself is racist," the statement read.

It came after the company's co-general manager, Rhys Lambert — the son of the director and former One Nation candidate Matthew Lambert — apologised for the driver's actions in the comments of an unrelated Provac Facebook post the day after the incident.

"To the driver involved, what happened to you was wrong, and I'm sorry," Mr Lambert wrote.

" It happened in our vehicle, on our time, by someone wearing our name. That's ours to answer for. "

In response to questions from the ABC, Provac Australia issued a statement through its lawyer, Cliff Savala, who said the company had "zero tolerance to racism, which it abhors in any shape or form".

Mr Savala said there were individuals "who have chosen to weaponise the alleged incident to deliberately and wilfully engage in both defamatory and offensive conduct".

Provac Australia did not respond to the ABC's question about whether the worker was still employed.

Gesture 'sad but not surprising'

Australia's Race Discrimination Commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, said racism had become more visible in society.

"We've seen an environment where parties with racist platforms are gaining popularity, where political rhetoric is openly embracing the White Australia policy," Mr Sivaraman said.

Giridharan Sivaraman says racism is becoming more prevalent in Australia. (Supplied: Giridharan Sivaraman)

He said he felt disheartened seeing politicians like Pauline Hanson referring to multiculturalism as a "failed policy" and felt it emboldened inflammatory debate.

"That rhetoric infects the population and spreads like a disease and leads to more overt racism on our streets," he said.

Mr Sivaraman said people who called out racism often faced greater consequences than alleged perpetrators of racism.

"It's one of the reasons people are scared to call out racism," he said.

Mr Sivaraman said there needed to be structural solutions to make it safe to report racism, like the National Anti-Racism Framework pitched by the Australian Human Rights Commission in 2024.

'We should be loud'

Ms Roberson said she had set up a fundraiser to pay for a lawyer.

Jessica Roberson says she had to call out the behaviour publicly. (Supplied: Jessica Roberson)

She said despite the looming threat of a lawsuit, she felt it was her duty, as a white Australian, to call out racist behaviour publicly.

"We should be loud. We have a privilege we should be using," she said.

Since posting the videos, Ms Roberson said she had heard from people across Australia who had witnessed or been subjected to similar racist incidents.

She said hearing from other people who spoke up publicly had "restored her faith in humanity".

title: Human tissue collected for biobank in fight against bowel cancer in young people
text:
Sunshine Coast researchers are building a 'biobank' of human tissue, as they investigate the increase in young people being diagnosed with bowel cancer.

They will collect tissue samples from patients under the age of 50 to look at whether modern living is to blame for the increase.

It's part of a collaboration between Sunshine Coast University Hospital (SCUH) and the University of the Sunshine Coast (UniSC).

UniSC cancer biologist Lochlan Fennell said they hoped to collect up to 60 samples over the next three years.

"We're going to study these tissues in extreme depth to try and understand if it is a new disease compared to traditional bowel cancer and also understand if we can treat it differently to improve patient outcomes," Dr Fennell said.

"We've done really well at reducing disease in people over 50, it's gone up by about 300 per cent over the past 30 years in patients aged under 50 years of age.

"This is really troubling because we don't actually know why that's occurred."

Researchers are looking into the increase in young people being diagnosed with bowel cancer. (Supplied: University of the Sunshine Coast)

Modern lifestyle impacts

Why are so many young people getting diagnosed with bowel cancer? Young people are more than twice as likely to get forms of bowel cancer than older Australians were at the same age, and researchers have a few clues as to why.

The $2.5 million research project will involve collecting both blood and tissue samples from patients being treated for early-onset bowel cancer at Sunshine Coast Health facilities.

Dr Fennell said researchers were hopeful of making some findings by the end of the year.

"Especially relating to if the disease is different to what we've seen traditionally," he said.

"We'll be able to do some analysis in the laboratory to really understand whether, at a real molecular level, it's the same sort of disease — but earlier — or if it's a completely different disease."

The research, funded by Cancer Australia and the National Health and Medical Research Council, will examine whether new lifestyle exposures are playing a part in the increase, including microplastics, chemicals and bacterial toxins.

Researchers will bank dozens of samples from bowel cancer patients under 50 to study the disease. (Supplied: University of the Sunshine Coast)

Increase in younger patients

According to Bowel Cancer Australia, it is the country's deadliest cancer for people aged between 25 and 54.

Sunshine Coast Health's acting medical director of Medical Oncology, Michael Allen, said 8-10 per cent of patients were now under the age of 40.

"There's often delays in diagnoses in younger patients because there is a misconception that young people don't get cancer, and what we're seeing is far from that," Dr Allen said.

"Symptoms can be very specific like bleeding, altered bowel habits, significant constipation, weight loss, it's unexplained, abdominal discomfort or bloating."

Natalie Hunter is a bowel cancer patient advocate. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast University Hospital)

Natalie Hunter was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer at 43 and is urging young people to take symptoms seriously.

"About three months before, I could see some changes in my bowel movements and didn't think anything of it because it was just over Christmas and thought I'd eaten too much or had too much to drink," she said.

Ms Hunter said she had been to see several GPs about her symptoms, who "kept saying I was too young" for anything to be wrong.

"Everything was OK until the tumour had blocked my bowel and then it was an emergency situation," she said.

She said she was in full support of the research project and continued to raise awareness about how the disease was impacting young people and trying to remove the stigma around the disease.

title: Broncos premiership prop announces medical retirement due to blood clots
text:
Brisbane Broncos premiership prop Corey Jensen has announced his medical retirement from the NRL after ongoing problems.

Jensen, who played 95 games for Brisbane including last year's grand final win over Melbourne Storm, also played 58 games in five seasons for North Queensland.

After becoming unwell during round seven, Jensen was diagnosed with a pulmonary embolism (blood clots in the lungs).

"After receiving medical advice and speaking to specialists, it's clear that it's no longer safe for me to play rugby league," he told reporters.

Jensen said he had been told he would have to take blood thinners for the rest of his life.

Big Ben heading to NFL The Brisbane Broncos are releasing forward Ben Te Kura from the rest of his NRL contract to allow him to pursue his dream of playing in the NFL.

"Since [the diagnosis] I've been able to train properly again, it's been like a mini pre-season, and I can do everything other than the contact, which is the frustrating part.

"Overall, my health's pretty good, I can continue training in the future and it's not going to affect me in any way."

The Broncos had confirmed he had another incident with deep vein thrombosis in his calf a year earlier, with both incidents considered unprovoked, meaning there was no obvious trigger such as a long-haul flight or injury.

"I leave with absolutely no regrets," he said, thanking his teammates for being part of the premiership win with them.

"I never chased individual recognition, but being part of a team, seeing people grow and knowing that in some way I may have contributed."

Corey Jensen played 95 games for the Broncos after joining the Brisbane side for the 2022 season. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Jensen teared up, thanking his wife Shannen for all her support and the sacrifices she had made.

"People see the player, but they don't always see what partners give up behind the scenes," he said.

Jensen is a qualified sports scientist, having completed a Bachelor of Sport and Exercise Science at James Cook University, and will have a bright future in that space if he chooses to pursue it.

Jensen was not a star as a youth but, through hard work, turned himself into a weapon after debuting for the Cowboys in 2017 and playing in the grand final.

"The late Paul Green gave me my debut back then.

"I was a bit of a late bloomer, so I'm grateful they took a punt on me, and I have to acknowledge how much the Cowboys did for my career," Jensen said.

"Coming down here was kind of a kind of a new lease on life. The Broncos gave me the opportunity, and I'm eternally grateful for what this club's done for me both on and off the field."

ABC/AAP

title: International military exercise Pitch Black draws in aviation enthusiasts
text:
Standing on a usually vacant block just off one of Darwin's busiest arterial roads, dozens of people point telescopic lenses towards the sky.

For the thousands of motorists who travel along Bagot Road in the Northern Territory capital every day, it has become quite the spectacle.

Until recently, many of these planespotters were strangers, with most travelling thousands of kilometres in the hope of capturing "the shot" of some of the world's fastest jet fighters participating in Exercise Pitch Black.

Dozens of people are out in Darwin this month to photograph planes taking part in the military exercise. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

For Melbourne-based aviation enthusiast Brian Carr, photographing the biennial event has been a dream come true.

"It's been on my list for many years because you get so many aircraft from so many different countries that you're just not going to see anywhere else," he said.

Brian Carr says attending Exercise Pitch Black in Darwin has been on his bucket list for a long time. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"You could probably go to half these countries and get arrested if you started looking at aeroplanes.

"Whereas here, you can come here and join hundreds of others and take some great photos."

Like most aviation nerds, Mr Carr's passion for big planes started at a young age with aspirations of ticking off serial numbers in collector books.

"I like my big things; ships, planes, boats," he said.

Brian Carr will document a plane's serial numbers from its photo. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"I like recording the serials on them, and you can't read them off; they're going too fast, and they're too far away generally, and they're very small.

"So yeah, take a photo, and you can look back at your leisure and work it out."

For other retirees, chasing air shows has almost become a full-time job.

Ian Rolfe has made the pilgrimage to Darwin all the way from the United Kingdom, "specifically for Pitch Black".

Ian Rolfe travelled all the way from the United Kingdom to come see Exercise Pitch Black. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"It's a massive opportunity for any aircraft enthusiasts to come out and see a variety of aircraft that you don't see in the UK or indeed in wider Europe," he said.

Mr Rolfe said the highlight of the three-week exercise so far was watching the Royal Australian Air Force's (RAAF) Super Hornet F/A-18 display at the Mindil Beach flyover.

Exercise Pitch Black 2026 takes flight Military aircraft and aviators from 20 countries land in Darwin ahead of Exercise Pitch Black 2026, with the biennial war games poised to begin.

Having traipsed around the globe photographing military planes since the 80s, he said Pitch Black ranked "very highly" compared with training exercises in other countries.

"It's a tribute to the Australian Air Force for making the facilities available and the fact they've managed to attract so many high-quality air forces, bringing some really interesting aircraft to the event," he told the ABC.

"Long may it continue."

While spotting interesting aircraft is the aim of the hobby, aviation enthusiasts say meeting like-minded people in their downtime is another drawcard.

Quinn Stanfield and Ben Goldsby say they really value the tight-knit community of aviation enthusiasts. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

Perth teenagers Ben Goldsby and Quinn Stanfield became fast friends while watching planes take off from their local airport.

"It's a very tight-knit community, everyone knows everyone," Mr Stanfield said.

"We're all very nice to each other, giving each other tips."

At just 14 years old, Mr Goldsby, a RAAF cadet, convinced his mum to miss a week of school to fly up to Darwin with his best friend to photograph the "sick" jet fighters for their social media followings.

Quinn Stanfield and Ben Goldsby travelled from Perth to Darwin to see the military exercise. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"We got friends, girls and boys, that come down and we just hang out in our group and just take the photos together, like check up on each other, you know, just hang out," he said.

"It's good fun as like a community, so somewhere where you belong."

As for those who are not yet official planespotters, there is still time, with the exercise continuing until August 6.

Recent aviation enthusiast Mary Chiron said she had become "obsessed" with taking her one-year-old son outside to look for jets for Pitch Black 2026.

Mary Chiron has started taking her son outside to watch the jets taking part in Exercise Pitch Black. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"I think this year I've just become really obsessed with them," she said.

"I'm always out searching for them because I want to get a nice close-up, but this is the first time that I've come and actually seen them a bit closer.

title: Quick hits: Swimmer spurns Love Island offer, dictator's grandson's vow
text:
A Scottish swimmer rejects an approach to appear on a dating reality show, Idi Amin's grandson reveals his royal plans and an Australian weightlifter adds to his family's medal history.

Here are the quick hits from day six of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Swimmer gives up Love Island opportunity

Scottish swimmer Katie Shanahan turned down an offer to appear on Love Island. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

Last year, Scottish swimmer Katie Shanahan had a choice to make.

Should she keep training with an eye on earning Commonwealth Games selection?

Or appear on reality dating program Love Island?

Shanahan spurned the chance to enter the villa and chose to focus on her swimming career and the decision is paying off.

The 22-year-old won silver in the women's 200m backstroke at the Glasgow Games.

"I'm the biggest Love Island fan ever. I've watched every season", Shanahan told BBC Scotland News.

"Last year the producers asked me and [English swimmer] Abbie Wood if we would be interested in doing it.

"I couldn't go on, though, because [I was] focusing on the swimming, but who knows in the future?

"I was a bit tempted but the swimming had to come first."

2. Idi Amin's grandson's vow

Aziz Abdul is disqualified during his bout on day six. (Reuters: Matthew Childs)

Carrying a family legacy into a sporting occasion can be a good thing.

In this instance, we're not sure it is.

Ugandan 90+kg boxer Aziz Abdul is the grandson of former Ugandan dictator Idi Amin.

Amin took charge in a coup in 1971 and ruled the country for eight years, during which an estimated half a million people were killed and the country's entire Asian population was expelled.

The Butcher of Uganda, as he was also known, had a bizarre fascination with Scotland, which was the subject of a film starring Forest Whitaker as Amin, The Last King Of Scotland.

It appears his grandson shares a similar love for the nation.

"In everything we do, God knows tomorrow," he told BBC Sport Scotland.

"It's God's plan. I might be the new king of Scotland. It's possible.

"When I arrived, I put up the flag, 'cause I like Scotland so much."

He fought England's Damar Thomas on day six in Glasgow but was disqualified for a headbutt during their quarterfinal.

3. Ollie's fall

Oliver Hoare falls during the mile heats. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Ollie Hoare suffered a major scare in the mile heats, falling half way through the race after appearing to be tripped.

"There was no-one in front of me and I fell down," Hoare later said in the mix zone.

"Tough to have that happen because obviously I wanted to compete on my own merit, and having something like that happen sucks.

"I got up and kept competing because that's what we do."

The Australian team immediately appealed to get Hoare into Saturday's final and were successful, meaning the worst of things for Hoare was a bit of track rash.

"I'm a bit scabbed up and feeling crap about it but we move on," he said.

He joins fellow Australians Adam Spencer and Cam Myer in the final.

4. Like father, like son

Oliver Saxton secured Commonwealth Games bronze in Scotland 40 years after his dad did the same. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

At the 1986 Edinburgh Commonwealth Games, English weightlifter Andrew Saxton claimed his first Commonwealth Games medal, a bronze in the 100kg sub-heavyweight division.

Forty years later, his son, Australian Ollie Saxton, achieved the same result in the 94kg division in Glasgow.

Saxton senior went on to win three golds in Auckland — back then you got a medal for the snatch, clean and jerk, and overall — something that would only earn him one medal today.

He represented England in those two Games, but four years after that, in Victoria, British Colombia, he won a silver for Australia.

Something for Ollie to aspire to in four years in Ahmedabad.

5. Bobsleigh 'bootcamp' for Welsh shot putter

Keeping busy during the athletics off-season is not a problem for Adele Nicoll.

The Welsh shot putter has one of the more unusual sporting crossover stories, mixing shot putt with bobsleigh.

And she's pretty good at both. In February she was flying down on the Pista Olimpica Eugenio Monti in Cortina d'Ampezzo at the 2026 Winter Olympics, where she finished 18th in the monobob and 15th in the two-woman.

She thinks the rigours and unglamorous life of a bobsled athlete places her in good stead for athletics.

"In athletics, we just get our kit bag and we turn up to the track, but with the bobsleigh we're driving the vans around the world," Nicoll told the BBC.

"You race, you pack up all the equipment and you drive to the next location, which could be a 24-hour journey.

Adele Nicoll competed in Milano-Cortina in the monobob and two-woman bobsleigh events. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

"It's just you and your teammates. You're doing all the servicing of the sleds, you're doing everything.

"Bobsleigh is basically a boot camp that makes you the most resilient, hard-working, grafting athlete.

"I've come back into athletics now with that discipline and that's what I think has made me a much better track and field athlete."

Nicoll finished fifth in the women's shot put today, AEST, with a best effort of 16.33m.

Nicoll is not the only crossover athlete to combine bobsledding with the Commonwealth Games.

Four-time medallist in track cycling from Birmingham 2022 and 2021 Tokyo Olympic sprint champion, Canadian Kelsey Mitchell, is also partial to bobsledding and finished 13th in the two-woman event in Cortina — and even acted as some inspiration for Aussie track cyclist Kristina Clonan.

title: Drive-in, drive-out health services helping regional students hear
text:
Two charities are working to close one of the biggest specialist healthcare gaps in regional Western Australia by delivering care and check-ups directly to schools.

Teach Hear Speak and Ear Health Australia have launched a three-year pilot program involving a bus, decorated by students, visiting schools across the state's Midwest.

The Buranymarda Marugundi Program, meaning "Good Strong Tomorrow" in Badimaya language, will deliver cost-free coordinated hearing health to address learning barriers.

Ear Foundation Australia founder Paul Higginbotham said the lack of access to care worsened further inland.

"The further east you go [from Geraldton] there's a challenge of delivering services into places like Meekatharra, Mount Magnet and Yalgoo," he said.

"We know there are kids right across this region who are sitting in classrooms and can't hear what's going on."

Paul Higginbotham says addressing hearing challenges in Aboriginal children is essential in closing the gap. (ABC News: Piper Duffy)

Mr Higginbotham said bringing services such as hearing check-ups to more remote communities could benefit future generations.

"You can't close the gap unless you can get a generation of kids through school," he said.

Children with hearing issues will be identified at school when services come to the area. (ABC News: Piper Duffy)

"And [currently] these kids can't get through school because the gunk in their ears is stopping them hearing.

" If you're sitting in a classroom ... regardless of your ethnicity you can't learn if you can't hear. "

Jasmin Mcaullay says bringing hearing check-ups to schools makes it convenient. (ABC News: Piper Duffy)

Checks helping families identify issues

Geraldton mother Jasmin Mcaullay found out her son Zaxson had ear congestion after a hearing check-up at school.

She said having services come to children rather than regional families having to seek them out made all the difference.

"I guess that's why the bus is so handy ... it makes it more convenient for mums to get [their kids ears] checked out," Ms Mcaullay said.

"I think it's really important for kids to have their ears checked."

Rangeway Primary School students created artwork which will decorate the 'ear bus'. (ABC News: Piper Duffy)

Teach Speak Hear chief executive Dr Carole Steketee said it was clear many factors were stopping regional families getting the help they need.

"There are barriers around cost, long wait times, long delays, long distance travel," she said.

Carole Steketee says distance is a barrier stopping families from getting developmental help. (ABC News: Piper Duffy)

"We can see there is an intergenerational impact because once we start seeing a child we don't release them from our register and we're constantly doing check-ins, adjusting supports according to their needs."

The pilot program is targeting 10 schools but Dr Steketee said there were plans to expand.

Dr Steketee says it is important to address hearing difficulties early in life. (ABC News: Piper Duffy)

"There's something like 40 odd schools in the region so this is just a drop in the ocean," she said.

"But it's a start and we hope through this program we start gathering the data and understanding what's working and what isn't."

Updated TechnologyTelecommunications Optus sued over Triple Zero outage linked to two deaths David Swan Updated July 30, 2026 — 12:11pm ,first published 11:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s communications regulator has sued Optus over last year’s Triple Zero outage, alleging the telco failed to connect emergency calls on 1005 occasions and exposing it to penalties of more than $250 million. The Australian Communications and Media Authority on Thursday filed civil penalty proceedings in the Federal Court against Optus Mobile over the September 18 outage, when a bungled firewall upgrade blocked calls to Triple Zero across South Australia, Western Australia, the Northern Territory and Far West NSW for about 13 hours. The outage was linked to two deaths. Australia’s communications regulator has sued Optus over last year’s Triple Zero outage. Getty Images The regulator alleges Optus Mobile broke the law twice over for each failed call: once by not giving callers access to the emergency call service, and again by not carrying those calls to the relevant termination point. The maximum penalty is $250,000 per contravention. ACMA chair Nerida O’Loughlin said the obligation was fundamental. “Australians rightly expect that when they call Triple Zero, their call will connect,” she said on Thursday. “Giving access to the emergency call service is not optional.”

Advertisement

Related Article Investigation

Telecommunications The emails that reveal how Optus downplayed the Triple Zero disaster Optus Mobile and other Singtel subsidiaries paid more than $12 million over similar failures in November 2023. O’Loughlin said the repeat so soon afterwards was a significant concern and a reason for going to court. An independent review by business veteran Kerry Schott made 21 recommendations and called the failures inexcusable, finding a 40-page crisis management document was too dense for staff to follow. Optus boss Stephen Rue, who kept his job, told a Senate inquiry Optus had a culture of carelessness, and has since moved call centre roles onshore, tightened escalation and replaced executives across network security, technology and risk. Communications Minister Anika Wells welcomed the action by the independent regulator and said the alleged failures were serious. “Australians rightly expect to reach Triple Zero when they need it most, and telcos are legally obligated to ensure that connection occurs,” Wells said. She declined to comment further while the matter is before the court.

Advertisement

An Optus spokesman said the company acknowledged the proceedings, but it would be inappropriate to comment on them. “Our focus remains on building a stronger and better Optus,” the spokesman said, pointing to continued investment in network resilience and a culture of transparency and accountability. Optus said the work was being supported by its transformation program and its implementation of the recommendations from the Schott review. Optus chief executive Stephen Rue appeared before a Senate inquiry intro Triple Zero in November. Alex Ellinghausen The proceedings land three weeks after Telstra’s nationwide outage on July 8, which affected more than 600 Triple Zero calls and left millions of customers without mobile services. No deaths have been linked to that failure, which the ACMA is separately investigating and which prompted the regulator to seek stronger powers to compel telcos to prove they have complied with the law.
