title: Gianni Infantino wants to sell off the World Cup. How can he be stopped?
text:
Advertisement

Analysis SportSoccerFIFA World Cup Gianni Infantino wants to sell off the World Cup. How can he be stopped? Sam Dean July 30, 2026 — 12:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The rebellion against Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in the World Cup has led to influential figures in football scrambling to oppose the FIFA president’s scheme. Infantino is an increasingly prominent figure on the world stage, thanks in no small part to his close relationship with Donald Trump, but that does not mean he is all-powerful. FIFA president Gianni Infantino’s proposal has met heated opposition. AP Here are the ways in which Infantino’s plot to sell the “soul” of football, as European governing body UEFA described it, could potentially be blocked. Kill the competition with a boycott

Advertisement

What would the World Cup be without European nations? It is a question that FIFA will have to consider should UEFA’s threat of a boycott materialise. Lobbying is already taking place to determine whether a European boycott could be agreed. The absence of European nations from the men’s and women’s World Cups would be a devastating blow to the competition. Five of the last six men’s World Cups have been won by European nations, and three of this year’s four World Cup semi-finalists were European. After all, both the men’s and women’s world champions are Spain. Gianni Infantino and US President Donald Trump console Lionel Messi after the World Cup final. AP The World Cup is regarded as the pinnacle of the game and much of its commercial appeal hinges on the presence of leading players. A boycott of European teams (and subsequent absence of many of the world’s top players) would undermine the competition at every level. The threat of a boycott has been used before. In 2021, UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin warned of a boycott by European and South American countries if FIFA pursued plans to stage the World Cup every two years. A few months later, Infantino backed away from the project, claiming it had never been proposed.

Advertisement

All 55 UEFA members would need to agree to a boycott, so it remains to be seen whether such drastic action is feasible. The early indications are that it might be difficult to convince all members to stand together on this issue. On Wednesday, the president of the Czech Republic’s football association said that he “can see the positive impact of FIFA’s intentions”. However, individual nations could take their own stand and refuse to play in FIFA competitions. Defeat Infantino in an election The next FIFA presidential election will take place in Rabat, Morocco, on March 18, 2027. Infantino confirmed in April that he will be standing for re-election, saying: “The last 10 years has been a pleasure and I am proud to have brought FIFA back to football and football back to FIFA. The journey goes on!” At the time of writing, Infantino is the only declared candidate. He also stood unopposed in 2019 and 2023. It had seemed improbable that anyone would stand against him next year, but the furious reaction to his latest scheme could yet change the situation. The deadline for other candidates to come forward is November 18, so there is enough time for rivals to organise themselves in response to these latest developments.

Advertisement

The problem faced by any potential rival to Infantino’s position is that he has seemingly already secured the votes required to win the election. Earlier this year, the South American, African and Asian confederations said they would back Infantino. Those three associations represent 111 countries, with Infantino needing the support of 106 of 211 member countries to win the vote. As of the spring, therefore, Infantino had effectively already won. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and FIFA boss Gianni Infantino ahead of the 2023 Women’s World Cup in Australia. Alex Ellinghausen Furthermore, Infantino has received support for re-election by other leading nations, including England. The Telegraph (London) revealed this month that England’s Football Association intended to back Infantino with a letter of endorsement after requests from FIFA to back his candidacy. The England FA refused to confirm whether that letter was sent, following the Folarin Balogun controversy at the World Cup. However, these associations could yet withdraw their support. The Asian Football Confederation said on Wednesday that it was “disappointed” that it was not consulted on Infantino’s proposal before it became public knowledge. The Asian body represents 47 votes, so a potential withdrawal of their support would open the door to another candidate. Who could stand against Infantino? Nasser Al-Khelaifi, the president of Paris St. Germain, has been touted as one potential option. Al-Khelaifi is deeply enmeshed in the world of football governance, as the chairman of European Football Clubs (EFC, previously known as the European Club Association) and an executive committee member of UEFA. He is the first Asian to hold a UEFA position, which could help him to win support from two continents.

Advertisement

On Wednesday, Al-Khelaifi’s EFC issued a statement to express its “serious concern” over FIFA’s actions over its private investment plans, and called for “calm and thorough consultation … with more rigorous and transparent governance processes put in place to protect the game for the long term”. ‘I am proud to have brought FIFA back to football and football back to FIFA.’ Gianni Infantino making a case for re-election as FIFA president It has also been reported that Dariusz Mioduski, the Polish owner and president of Legia Warsaw, may be a potential rival to Infantino. Mioduski is also an EFC vice-president. Victor Montagliani, the president of CONCACAF and vice-president of FIFA, has not ruled out a future run for the presidency, although he is expected to seek re-election with CONCACAF next year. Infantino and FIFA did find some support in Africa. The Confederation of African Football did not criticise the plans and instead asked its members to participate in consultation. It will hold a committee next week to “assess and evaluate the proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise.”

Advertisement

US President Donald Trump and FIFA president Gianni Infantino after the World Cup final. AP Dial up the political pressure Even before this latest move, Infantino had been dealing with increasingly intense scrutiny as a consequence of his close relationship with the Trump administration. Earlier this week, for example, a leading Democratic lawyer wrote to Infantino to request he appear before the House judiciary committee. Representative Jamie Raskin, the senior member on the committee, has requested FIFA to provide all of its records on its contacts with Trump, his administration and The Trump Organisation, the family business. Raskin put Infantino and FIFA on notice not to destroy or delete any correspondence with Trump and his associates and requested he produce “a list of anything of value (including transfer of money, gifts, prizes, awards, or public appearances) given to President Trump, members of his administration, or their family members, or any entity associated with them, such as The Trump Organisation”.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

Mergers & acquisitions ‘Nuclear bomb’: FIFA president’s plan to sell World Cup stake met with fury The Democrats are the minority in the House, meaning Raskin is unlikely to have the power to force Infantino to appear. But that could change should the Democrats retake control in the next midterms, which would potentially give him the power to subpoena the FIFA president to answer questions. Infantino’s attempts to cosy up to Trump have long been clear to the watching world, but the apparent partnership between the two men triggered criticism during the World Cup, as a result of the Balogun scandal. Trump said he asked FIFA to review the US forward’s one-match ban, which was subsequently suspended. As a consequence, 72 members of the European Parliament called for an investigation into Infantino’s role in the Balogun decision. The spotlight on Infantino’s relationship with the Trump administration will now become more intense. The proposed investor group will be led by Thrive Capital, which is run by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

Advertisement

Sources have played down suggestions of involvement by the Trump administration in the plans, but these family links will not ease the political pressure facing Infantino. Andy Burnham, the new UK prime minister, has criticised the latest proposals, while other politicians and activists have also raised their voices in opposition to the new plot. Glenn Micallef, the European commissioner for intergenerational fairness, youth, culture and sport, made clear his objections on Wednesday. “The relentless commercialisation of football has become corrosive,” he said. “It’s threatening the things that made football the world’s most popular sport.” Infantino’s opponents will hope that the rising tide of political anger will help to convince member associations to turn their backs on Infantino. title: As the Fed sits tight on interest rates, investors take action

Kevin Warsh, the Trump-appointed chair of the US Federal Reserve Board, talks like a hawk, but has yet to act as one. That’s left it to investors to take matters out of his - and the Fed’s - hands. Long-term bond yields shot up – the 30-year yield to its highest level since 2007 – and Wall Street slumped after the Fed left US interest rates unchanged and Warsh provided no guidance in his press conference on the future direction of the Fed’s policy rate. No predictions: US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh is staying mum on the outlook for interest rates. AP There is some pressure for a rate rise building with the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) that sets US monetary policy. For the first time in a decade, three of its members – three regional Fed presidents – voted for a 25 basis point rate hike. Warsh, however, while continuing to assert that he has “no tolerance” for elevated inflation levels – the US inflation rate has remained above the Fed’s 2 per cent target for more than five years – maintained his stance of providing no guidance to market participants, saying only that “we’re on the job, we will deliver.” How and when the Fed might deliver were left as open questions.

Advertisement

The lack of guidance is deliberate. He has said he wants financial markets to respond to economic developments, rather than the Fed’s signalling, and become a “direct and unfiltered” source of information for the Fed. That is effectively what he got. The markets, the bond market in particular, took matters into their own hands, with the spike in yields on the longer duration bonds effectively tightening US monetary policy despite the Fed leaving rates unchanged. The bond market is providing Warsh with the signal he wants: it is saying that it is now questioning whether he is as committed to attacking inflation as he has claimed. While the yield on two-year US Treasury notes – the securities that are most sensitive to movements, or expectations of movement, in the federal funds rate – actually fell, the yield on 10-year bonds jumped 7 basis points to 4.68 per cent, and that on 30-year bonds rose 11 basis points to 5.2 per cent. The bond market is providing Warsh with the signal he wants: it is saying that it is now questioning whether he is as committed to attacking inflation as he has claimed.

If he won’t act to protect the holders of the securities most threatened by heightened inflation levels, they’ll act to protect themselves and raise the rates that have the most influence on US businesses and consumers. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump’s America is sinking as his war on the world sputters Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The Fed, of course, has been under intense pressure from Donald Trump since he regained the White House and renewed the demands for rate cuts that were a feature of his first term as president, although this time they have included active efforts to gain control of the Fed’s board. His administration has targeted former Fed chair Jerome Powell and another governor, Lisa Cooke, with transparently political prosecutions to remove them and create an opening for Trump nominees. Asked about the central bank’s decision to hold rates steady, Trump didn’t criticise Warsh.

Advertisement

“I know he’d love to see lower interest rates, but he’s got a board, and it’s a political board, and they want to keep rates up,” he said. The dissent from the majority decision by the three regional Fed presidents and comments by other Fed officials in the lead-up to the meeting suggest that, had Warsh maintained the previous Fed policy of providing some guidance in its official statement on monetary conditions, it would have reflected a bias towards raising rates. The markets, which wouldn’t have been shocked had there been a rate hike at this week’s meeting, are now pencilling one in September, with a further increase possible in December. If that were to eventuate, Warsh might well find himself also targeted by Trump, given the political implications of a rate rise in the lead-up to America’s midterm elections in November. A Democrat majority in the House alone could neuter Trump’s presidency, while exposing him and his family to congressional investigations and, almost inevitably, more impeachment proceedings.

Advertisement

After sitting back and watching the US inflation rate since the start of the year – the Fed has left the federal funds rate unchanged at its past five meetings – the members of the FOMC ought to have a bias towards raising rates. While the headline consumer price index rate did fall last month for the first time in five months (to 3.5 per cent), the measure the Fed places most weight on – the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index – was 4.1 per cent in May, the most recent monthly data available. “Core” PCE, which excludes volatile energy and food prices, edged up from 3.3 per cent to 3.4 per cent. That’s well above the Fed’s target, and moving in the wrong direction. Since the start of the Iran war, US consumers have been grappling with soaring fuel prices. AP When Trump regained the presidency in January last year, the headline PCE rate was 2.5 per cent, the core rate 2.6 per cent and the Fed had cut rates three times, by 25 basis points each time.

Advertisement

Since then, Trump’s tariffs, his “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” with its massive tax cuts and increased spending, and the war on Iran have caused the rate to jump. The war in the Middle East, in particular, has had a marked impact. When Joe Biden handed over the White House, the national average gasoline price was $US3.11 a gallon and diesel averaged $3.76 a gallon. On February 27 this year, a day before the US and Israel attacked Iran, the average gasoline price was just under $US3 a gallon and diesel still $US3.76 a gallon. Today, those prices are around $US4.09 and $US5.33 a gallon, respectively. The Fed has, so far, seemed to have believed that Trump’s tariffs would create a one-off hit to the inflation rate and then, with those costs absorbed, their effects would disappear from the data. There may have been similar thoughts about the effects of a war that Trump boasted would be over within days.

Advertisement

Despite having made two different attempts to impose a global tariff regime that were deemed illegal by the courts, Trump is persevering with his third attempt, while also regularly announcing new tariffs as retaliation for other countries’ policies, or punishment for perceived insults. The tariffs – a de-facto tax on US businesses and consumers – are continuing to impact the inflation rate. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Will the AI boom lead to lower interest rates? Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Despite Trump’s numerous declarations of victory, the conflict in the Middle East continues and is entering its sixth month. Oil prices remain high, at around $US90 a barrel, and the longer the war continues and oil flows from the Persian Gulf remain restricted, the greater the likelihood that the inflationary effects will spread from fuel prices to the cost of goods and become baked into the inflation rate and expectations of future inflation. The same could be said of Trump’s tariffs.

Advertisement

The inflation rate is also being boosted by the extraordinary boom in investment in artificial intelligence and the infrastructure to support it, which has driven up semiconductor and other IT equipment prices along with construction and energy costs. In the long run, AI might lift productivity rates without fanning inflation. In the near term, and perhaps well beyond, it is contributing to an inflation rate that is well above the level that the Fed, and Warsh, have declared they will tolerate. The Fed made the mistake in the aftermath of the pandemic of regarding the inflationary effects of the global supply chain disruptions as “transitory.” There are plenty of members of the FOMC – including Jerome Powell, who has hung on as a governor while waiting for unequivocal evidence that the administration is longer pursuing him – who won’t want to make the same mistake twice. Even if they were inclined to extend the period of watching and waiting and gathering more data before the next meeting in September, their inaction, and the absence of any guidance, has forced the markets to come to its own conclusions about the inflation outlook and take action itself. title: Why this philosopher thinks the past is like a zoo
text:
Advertisement

CultureBooksTake 7 Why this philosopher thinks the past is like a zoo Kylie Northover July 30, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hanno Sauer is an associate professor of philosophy at the Department of Philosophy and Religious Studies at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, where he teaches ethics, metaethics and political philosophy. Often considered controversial for his provocative ideas around human morality and criticism of historical philosophy, his accessible books on philosophy have been widely acclaimed. Next month, he’s in Australia where he’ll be challenging the political belief that a truly classless society can ever be achieved, and discussing his latest book, The Invention of Good and Evil: A World History of Morality, exploring the evolutionary story behind humanity’s moral transformations over the past 500 years. German philosopher, author and night owl Hanno Sauer. Worst habit? Going to bed late. I don’t like getting up in the morning and I enjoy the nights - I read, and I watch another movie. If you are like me, then you know society is prejudiced against us and biased in favour of early risers. We should split up - we should have two societies.

Advertisement

Greatest fear? My deepest fear is that harm will come to my children, of course. Another - and this may seem silly, but I am serious - is that when I accepted this invitation [to Australia], I had a long back-and-forth with various people asking what’s the probability I will encounter a non-European spider? I am very arachnophobic; it’s my biggest irrational fear. Another is that everything becomes slightly more shitty, slowly, and we can’t escape it. It feels like it’s already happening - public infrastructure decays, and it gets grandfathered in and everyone just accepts it. I know I’m supposed to say climate change and fascism and so on, but personally, I will say that slow, gradual, hard-to-notice inconvenience and dysfunction of things around me. I’m 42 now, so it may just be that I’m getting grumpy, but I do think things used to work better.

Advertisement

Francis Bacon’s 1953 work Study after Velazquez’s Portrait of Pope Innocent X. Alamy Stock Photo The line that stayed with you? I always liked this from a very obscure 18th-century German writer and philosopher, Georg Christoph Lichtenberg, who said, “philosophy is a bit like shaving – you shouldn’t practise it in your throat”. It means that you shouldn’t start with dangerous questions. Biggest regret? I should have learnt to play an instrument, but I never really liked doing things that didn’t come naturally to me. More seriously, my mother’s father died before I was born, and my father’s father was a drinker - he was morose, so I didn’t enjoy spending time with him. But then my grandmother on my mother’s side met a partner later in life, and I loved him and spent quite a bit of time with him. When I was at university, in the first semester, he got cancer. He was in the hospital and … I was just too young, and I didn’t want to confront the fact that he was dying, and I didn’t visit him. I had a phone call with him and … he knew he was dying and that I really liked him, but I didn’t convey that to him sufficiently. I should have been less scared. That was a mistake and I didn’t handle that well.

Advertisement

Tell us about your turning point? Originally, I wanted to be a novelist. I wanted to write the Great American novel but whatever the German version of that is - that was my vision when I was about 14 or 15 because I loved reading and that romantic vision of a bohemian lifestyle. That didn’t happen but the idea of writing non-academically stayed with me - to write books that reach a wider audience. And there came a point in my life when I felt like it’s now or never, so I contacted an acquaintance of mine and asked him, how do I approach this, how do I get published? That was in 2020, and that changed my life. The books have been very successful, and I have got to meet so many interesting, influential and charismatic people, and I’m travelling all the time and I get into controversies - I enjoy that. The artwork or song you wish was yours? In terms of owning and having produced it, I would like one of Francis Bacon’s paintings. It would be financially very lucrative, but also, I love his work from when I first saw an exhibition of his pope paintings in Basel in Switzerland when I was 17. They had Bacon’s popes and also Diego Velázquez’s painting (Portrait of Pope Innocent X) that Bacon was referring to, and it was awesome. So I would like an upsetting Francis Bacon painting.

Advertisement

Related Article Take 7 ‘We sent the tech bros to Mars’: The story Anna Funder most wants to tell If you could time travel, where would you choose to go? How long do I have to stay? What can I bring? I don’t want to spend a night in medieval England, it’s super dangerous. I couldn’t survive 24 hours in ancient Rome - I don’t know anyone and I don’t speak the language. Where do I sleep? I’m curious, but it’s too dangerous! I think this question is like asking, which cage in the zoo would you like to be teleported into? None! Most would be too small for me and I could be crushed, or they would contain dangerous animals, or some would be underwater, and I would have to swim, and it wouldn’t be fun. I think the past is like a zoo, and it contains many cages that I’m not interested in visiting. Maybe I would go back to have lunch with (German philosopher) Nietzsche, but I’m sceptical. I’m sticking with the past as a zoo, and I’m not into it. Hanno Sauer appears at The Wheeler Centre Melbourne as part of The Fifth Estate series on August 20, where he will discuss his latest book and at the Festival of Dangerous Ideas in Sydney (August 20-30), where he will appear in several panels.

title: Zelenskyy tells Ukrainians to brace for 'massive' Russian attack following oil refinery strikes
text:
In Brief Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday there was a "high probability" that a "massive" Russian strike would be carried out imminently.

The Ukrainian president met with US President Donald Trump at the White House on Wednesday.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday that Russia would likely carry out another massive attack on the country overnight, in a message posted on social media.

"The Russians prepared a massive attack several days ago, and there is a high probability that the strike will be carried out tonight," he said in a post on X.

"Please, in all regions of Ukraine, pay attention to air raid alerts today and stay safe."

Ukrainian drones hit oil refineries and logistics facilities in the Russian cities of Perm, Ryazan and Taganrog, as well as the Crimean peninsula, on Wednesday, with the country's top online retailer Wildberries evacuating its Ryazan warehouse.

While Ukraine's air defences are running low on interceptors like Patriot missiles, leaving it more exposed to Russian strikes, its own deep-strike drone production has outpaced Russia's, enabling it to hit Russian oil refineries and infrastructure and cause fuel shortages across its 11 time zones.

title: The $67 million journalism fund claim against Labor — and what the facts show
text:
In brief The Journalism Assistance Fund is a $67.6 million federal government program that subsidises the wages of more than 2,000 journalists at 185 media organisations.

It has sparked debate over independence and editorial influence.

Claims that the federal government is using taxpayer money to bankroll media outlets for favourable coverage have spread online, sparking debate about press independence.

The Journalism Assistance Fund (JAF), launched last November, is a $67.6 million federal government program that subsidises the wages of more than 2,000 journalists at 185 news publishers across Australia.

Critics, including News24 (formerly known as Sky News) commentator Andrew Bolt, say the scheme could influence how outlets cover the government.

But the government says the fund is designed to support public-interest journalism, promote media diversity and help newsrooms navigate ongoing disruption across the media sector.

So what is the JAF, who received the money, and do the criticisms stack up?

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What is the Journalism Assistance Fund?

The JAF is a key part of the federal government's broader News Media Assistance Program, announced in 2024 and designed to support public-interest journalism and media diversity.

It provides grants to eligible Australian organisations that publish digital "core news content" that reports, investigates or explains issues relevant to informing democratic decision-making or current events of public significance.

Lifestyle, entertainment, celebrity, real estate and sponsored content are excluded, as are opinion and editorial pieces.

The grants subsidise part of the cost of employing full-time journalists, providing up to $13,000 per journalist each year, or $39,000 over the three-year life of the program.

According to the funding guidelines, the program aims to support Australian news publishers and the continued employment of journalists producing public-interest journalism.

The government says the scheme was in response to years of financial pressure on the news industry, as publishers face declining advertising revenue, newsroom closures and increasing competition from digital platforms such as Alphabet and Meta.

In a speech last week, Communications Minister Anika Wells said the fund was about sustaining public-interest journalism across Australia and rejected suggestions it could influence editorial decisions.

Communications Minister Anika Wells rejected suggestions the fund would influence editorial decisions. Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

"This support is not conditional on what stories are written, and anything to the contrary is an insult to Australian journalists. Our media sector is strong and mature and I know they do and will continue to hold people to account, including those in government," she said.

The funding guidelines do not require outlets to acknowledge receipt of program funding, but state that, if an acknowledgement is included, it should state that the funding "does not influence the production of specific content".

Only Australian-owned or controlled news organisations meeting the eligibility criteria could apply.

Applications were assessed on a first-come, first-served basis, with the program closing less than a month after the available funding was exhausted.

In total, 185 Australian news publishers received funding, including 93 regional publishers, 23 culturally and linguistically diverse publishers, 22 suburban publishers and two First Nations publishers.

Who received the funding?

The largest grants went to Australia's major commercial media companies.

Nine was the largest beneficiary, receiving $16.1 million across two grants.

The largest individual grant ($8.16 million) went to Fairfax Media Limited, which publishes The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age and The Australian Financial Review. Nine acquired Fairfax in 2018, but the grant was listed under Fairfax Media Limited.

Nine Entertainment, which includes the company's television network, received a further $7.96 million.

Seven West Media was given a total of $11.33 million, with its television network receiving $5.6 million.

However, many independent and regional publishers also received funding.

SA Today, which owns regional South Australian newspapers, received $2.7 million.

Regional Publishers, which owns The Courier in Ballarat, received $2.28 million. The Conversation received $1.03 million, while dozens of smaller regional and community news organisations also received grants.

Foreign-owned publishers, including News Corp and The Guardian Australia, were ineligible under the scheme. The ABC and SBS were also excluded because they already receive public funding.

The full list of organisations that received funding, along with the amounts, is publicly available on GrantConnect.

Why has the fund become controversial?

One News Nation, which describes itself as an independent "centre-right" news outlet, appeared to be the first to report the full list of recipients last week.

According to an ABC News Verify investigation, the outlet publishes pro-One Nation content and its social media page recently rebranded from the "One Nation Supporters Network", though it denies it is affiliated with the party.

In social media posts, the outlet accused the government of "quietly paying journalist wages" and claimed Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was deciding "who counts as news".

READ MORE How to check your offset account is working properly after $55 million error exposed

The posts received thousands of likes, with many comments accusing the government of "bribing" the media for favourable coverage.

Bolt also criticised the program, saying funded organisations should disclose the government support.

"I'm not saying all these journalists toe the Labor line as a result of the money, but shouldn't they at least declare this government money at the bottom of every one of their articles?" he asked.

He added: "I think it's a corrupting influence because it makes journalists and media outlets look to the government and not want to offend the government."

In a separate News24 segment, Rita Panahi claimed the funds were mostly flowing to left-wing media outlets.

Does government funding influence journalism?

Media experts say the central question is whether funding journalism is different from funding editorial content.

Joanne Gray, chair of discipline, media and communications at the University of Sydney, said she thought it was unlikely the recipients were coming under political influence of the government, and there has been no evidence that recipients have altered their editorial coverage because of the grants.

"Governments often fund news and journalism through various models, and it's common throughout the world, and it's common in Australia," she told SBS News.

"As long as the funds are transparent and people are adhering to journalistic standards, and they're reviewing it, I don't see funds having or causing a problem of bias or being politicised or being misused for political reasons."

Matthew Ricketson, a communications professor at Deakin University, said he believed criticisms that the funds could influence editorial content were a "half-truth".

"If government is funding the media, there are certainly things to look out for and be wary of," he said.

But he said publicly funded broadcasters such as the ABC and SBS had maintained their independence.

"I'd add that newspapers, whether online or historically in print, have received government advertising for well over 100 years," he told SBS News.

"Nobody seriously has argued that has unduly influenced those newspapers to write positive things about governments when they didn't want to."

A spokesperson from the Department of Communications said the federal government believed "a strong, sustainable and diverse news sector is a critical element of a healthy democracy — supporting an informed citizenry and social cohesion".

"As part of the News Media Assistance Program, the Journalism Assistance Fund supports news organisations to keep journalists employed and produce public interest news that informs Australians," the spokesperson said.

"As with all Government grant processes, funding was awarded following assessment against eligibility criteria stated in the Grant Guidelines available at business.gov.au.

"The grant was open to all Australian-based news organisations that produce core news content that is digitally distributed."

title: Treasurer welcomes 'encouraging' numbers as inflation falls to pre-war level
text:
In brief Housing remained the biggest contributor to inflation in the June figures.

The Reserve Bank is due to meet on 10 and 11 August to make its next interest rate decision.

An unexpected drop in Australia's inflation has eased fears of another imminent interest rate hike.

The latest Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data showed headline inflation — the total inflation rate in an economy, including volatile items like fuel — falling from 4 per cent to 3.8 per cent in June.

It's now at its lowest level since 28 February, when the US and Israel launched an attack on Iran.

Trimmed mean inflation — which measures underlying inflation without volatile items and is the preferred measure by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) — remained steady at 3.6 per cent, defying central bank predictions of a rise to 3.8 per cent.

The fall in inflation coincided with transport costs moderating for the month, ABS head of price statistics Rachel McCrick said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Lower world oil prices as a result of some stabilisation in the Middle East in June contributed to fuel prices falling 10.9 per cent in the month," she said on Wednesday.

"The federal government's fuel excise relief measures, which contributed to lower automatic fuel prices in April and May, also remained in place."

The fuel excise measures reduced the cost of fuel by 32 cents a litre during the month.

However, the measure was reduced to just 16 cents in July, and will be phased out entirely from Sunday.

Source: SBS News

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the inflation figures were reassuring following a period of economic volatility.

"It's an encouraging outcome that shows we've made progress on inflation since the budget, even in the face of intense global uncertainty," he said.

"Treasury has warned that the next phase of the conflict could be more challenging for the global economy, with the oil market now more vulnerable."

Quarterly inflation numbers showed headline inflation falling from 4 to 3.9 per cent.

Meanwhile, the trimmed mean rose from 3.5 per cent in the March quarter to 3.6 per cent in the June quarter.

READ MORE Drivers warned about key dates as government confirms fuel discount's end

Housing remained the biggest contributor to inflation in the June monthly figures, rising by 6.8 per cent.

"Annual inflation for new dwellings has reached its highest level in almost three years, at 5.8 per cent," McCrick said.

"This was driven by builders passing on higher material and labour costs."

How will new inflation numbers impact interest rates?

The head of economic research at Oxford Economics Australia, Harry Murphy Cruise, said the RBA would be focused less on the headline figures and more on the breadth of price rises.

"Underlying inflation is not just resisting pressure to rise. In quarterly terms, it is continuing to ease," he said.

"All that backs up our view that the RBA will keep rates on hold next month."

The RBA is due to meet on 10 and 11 August to decide whether interest rates will rise from current levels of 4.35 per cent, or keep them on hold.

READ MORE Albanese flags new fuel announcements as petrol prices tipped to spike further

The bank's governor, Michele Bullock, said on Tuesday that higher interest rates were slowing the economy as expected.

The past four years of above-target inflation had been a cautionary tale for the Reserve Bank board, she said.

"The longer it is out of target, the more concerned that the board becomes," Bullock told a fundraising lunch at the Anika Foundation in Sydney.

"It is quite at the front of their minds. In the May forecast we had it coming back under 3 [per cent] towards the end of 2027, and that's a long time to be above target."

title: Drivers warned about key dates as government confirms fuel discount's end
text:
In Brief Treasurer Jim Chalmers has confirmed the fuel excise discount will end on 2 August.

Drivers can expect prices to rise by a "few cents per litre" starting Monday.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has confirmed the fuel excise discount will end on Sunday 2 August, ending weeks of uncertainty over whether the discount would be extended for a second time.

"It was never the government's intention for [the discount] to be permanent," Chalmers said on Wednesday.

The initial discount of 32c per litre ended in June, after which the government extended the fuel excise cut at a reduced rate of 16c per litre.

"We began to taper that off at the start of the month, deliberately, so that we could provide a bit more cost of living help," Chalmers said.

While the NRMA does expect a modest rise in petrol prices from Monday, the roadside assistance and travel organisation doesn't expect costs to skyrocket.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Our message to the public is: We know fuel prices are going to go up on Monday and beyond. We don't know by how much," NRMA spokesperson Peter Khoury told SBS News.

"We would expect average prices to go up a few cents per litre ... but it really depends on the service station."

Companies showing 'restraint'

The announcement ended weeks of uncertainty over whether the government would extend the fuel excise discount after Iran resumed its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, sending global oil markets into shock for the second time since the US-Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic in February.

Khoury said global oil markets were already responding to news on Monday that both sides had halted bombing, with benchmark unleaded prices dropping.

If the relative calm continues, Khoury said it will "definitely negate the increases we're going to get from the tax being reintroduced".

"We've seen a lot of restraint from the oil companies in the past few weeks," he said, adding that if global oil prices continued to fall it would "cushion the blow" of upcoming price rises in Australia.

By how much will prices go up?

Khoury said that price rises caused by the end of the fuel excise discount wouldn't happen overnight.

"It will be gradual, it won't be immediate," he said.

"Not every service station is going to put their price up by 17 cents a litre. In fact, almost none will. So please don't go out and panic buy."

Khoury told SBS News that, by the time the discount expires, it's likely the increase will be closer to 17 cents rather than the extended excise reduction rate of 16 cents.

"We think it's going to be another cent because of the inflation adjustment, which also just happens to land on the same day [Monday] they do that twice a year."

Just how much cost will be passed on to the consumer depends on individual service stations, Khoury added.

"We don't want people to panic because some service stations will go up on Monday and others won't; it really depends on when they sell their stock."

In any case, the fuel excise discount is being wound up against the backdrop of retail prices that are already steadily rising.

"The national average for unleaded is about $1.93, and we're expecting that to continue to increase based on the increases we've seen for wholesale prices," Khoury said.

That's a 13-cent increase from the $1.80 per litre calculated by the Australian Consumer and Competition Commission as the average petrol price in major cities on 22 July.

As of 21 July, Australia has 42 days of fuel reserves, with an expected 3.1 billion litres of crude, diesel, jet fuel, and petrol scheduled to arrive over the next four weeks, according to the federal government.

title: Could Qantas' record-breaking new plane make stopovers a thing of the past?
text:
In brief A record-breaking Qantas flight has flown for more than 24 hours as part of the airline's bid to offer nonstop flights to London.

But experts say the ultra-long-haul flight isn't necessarily a replacement for flights with stopovers.

A record-breaking test flight lasting more than 24 hours has touched down in France from Melbourne — and experts say Australia could be leading the world on the new technology use.

Qantas' specially adapted Airbus A350-1000ULR landed in France on Tuesday after a marathon 24 hours and 24 minutes in the air, covering 23,057km without stopping — the longest direct flight ever attempted by a commercial aircraft.

The flight is part of a two-month test campaign as part of Qantas' Project Sunrise, which aims to launch the world's longest commercial passenger flight and reshape long-haul travel by offering direct flights from Australia's east coast to London and New York.

The previous record belonged to a Boeing 777-200LR, which flew 21,601.7km from Hong Kong to London in 22 hours and 42 minutes back in 2005.

Qantas has ordered 12 of the modified A350 aircraft, each fitted with an extra 20,000-litre fuel tank and configured to seat 238 passengers.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The first is due for delivery in April 2027, with daily non-stop flights between Sydney and London planned from October that year — turning what was once a five-day journey in 1947 on the old 'Kangaroo Route' into a single hop of 19 to 21 hours, depending on winds and routing.

The airline has said a Sydney-New York route will follow shortly after the launch of the London route.

Could stopovers become a thing of the past?

The test flight's success has cast eyes towards the future of air travel, with some wondering whether stopovers in Singapore, Dubai or Los Angeles may be a thing of the past.

But that's not quite where we're headed, experts say.

Justin Brownjohn from RMIT University's Aviation Academy says non-stop routes will keep becoming more viable as aircraft range improves and fuel use falls — but that doesn't make them a replacement for one-stop flying.

"Airlines have historically competed on network and frequency, but Project Sunrise competes on time," he said.

READ MORE Where Australian luxury travellers are heading in 2026 — and what it could cost

"Cutting up to four hours off the journey from Sydney to London and removing the connection entirely is a different product, not an improved version of the existing one.

"These services won't replace one-stop flying, they'll sit alongside it."

Brownjohn expects the strongest demand for the ultra-long-haul services to come from business and premium leisure travellers willing to pay more for the time saved — and says the wider effect may be felt most by the Middle Eastern and Asian hub airports that have built their business models around the layover.

'A different physiological event'

Spending over 20 hours in the air also raises real questions about passenger wellbeing.

"Twenty hours is not a longer flight, it is a different physiological event," Brownjohn said. "On this flight comfort has stopped being a luxury feature and become the thing being sold."

Peter Cistulli, professor of sleep medicine at the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre, worked with Qantas on the physiological side of the aircraft's design.

Qantas' Project Sunrise envisions nonstop long-haul flights. Source: AAP / James Ross

"Project Sunrise takes ultra-long-haul flights to a whole new level," Cistulli told SBS News.

"It's arguably the final frontier of travel on Earth, so it brings a whole lot of additional challenges, including the biological challenge of crossing so many time zones over a short period and how that can influence your health and wellbeing."

Cistulli, who also worked with the airline on its long-haul Dreamliner aircraft, said compressing so many time zones into one flight leaves the body's circadian system less time to adjust.

He says researchers' input on elements including lighting, meal timing, and in-flight exercise is intended to help passengers adapt to their destination time zone faster.

The aircraft has what Qantas describes as the lowest seat density of any comparable jet, with more than 40 per cent of the 238 seats allocated to premium cabins.

A wellness zone will also offer stretch handles, refreshments, and a guided, video-led movement program.

But Cistulli is also candid about the risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), with long periods of immobility already proven to raise DVT risk.

While he says the baseline risk on any flight is already low at under 1 per cent, those with "heightened risk" of DVT may not be suitable for the ultra-long-haul flight.

For the average person, however, concerns about the lengthy flight can be mitigated by adequate physical activity on board.

He says that opting for stopovers has both its pros and cons when it comes to health. Being able to get off a flight and move around in an airport is a benefit, he says, but that also adds to the journey and can increase fatigue.

"Of course, not everybody would choose to be cooped up in a plane for 20-plus hours — the stopover options will always remain there. Passengers will have their choice."

Australia's shrinking distance problem

Cistulli sees Project Sunrise as part of Australia's long fight against the "tyranny of distance" it's grappled with as a geographically isolated nation.

"This is the ultimate frontier, in that we're bringing the world closer to Australia and Australia closer to the world," he says. "It's a really fantastic story for Australia, and it's no surprise that an Australian airline would go to the trouble of solving this problem."

READ MORE A travel charge most Australians don't know they pay is rising again

Whether Qantas holds onto the bragging rights is another question.

Singapore Airlines already operates the world's longest scheduled commercial route — a roughly 19-hour service between Singapore and New York.

"I think it will be interesting to see what the competition do," he says. "This will definitely give Qantas a competitive advantage, but whether that's long-lived, time will tell."

The extended range also opens up more than just one route. With planes capable of covering these distances, almost any city pairing becomes commercially viable if there's demand for it.

READ MORE 'Unpredictable': New warning for Australians travelling abroad

It also gives Qantas more flexibility to route around trouble spots, including current airspace restrictions due to the war in the Middle East, opening up options such as flying to London over the North Pole instead.

Cistulli is careful to frame Project Sunrise as an addition to the market, not a replacement for it.

"I think it's all about choice, and tailoring the opportunity for particular customer needs," he said. "This just adds a new option for people who do need to get somewhere in a hurry, so to speak — and I think that's a great addition."

title: How to check your offset account is working properly after $55 million error exposed
text:
IN BRIEF A review by ASIC found banks paid over $55 million in customer compensation for offset account failures.

Experts said Australians should check whether their offset account has been set up and managed correctly.

Australians have lost millions of dollars to offset account errors, according to a review by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC).

The corporate regulator analysed the offset practices of eight banks, which it said represent more than 70 per cent of Australia's $2.5 trillion home loan market.

It found weaknesses in how all banks established, monitored and managed offset accounts.

Reports to ASIC between September 2023 and August 2025 showed that banks paid over $55 million in customer compensation for offset account failures.

In some cases, customers were repaid over $17,000 due to system limitations or administrative errors.

What exactly is an offset account?

Offset accounts operate like everyday transaction accounts, which can be used to deposit and withdraw money. But they're often marketed as a simple way to reduce home loan interest.

That's because money held in an offset account also reduces the outstanding amount owed on a home loan, which is used to calculate the interest paid on that loan.

If a person has $50,000 in their offset account and a $750,000 loan, they will only be charged interest on $700,000.

Source: SBS News

Sally Tindall, director of data insights at Canstar, said offset accounts are a popular choice for many Australian mortgage holders.

"For many customers, it's one of the most powerful tools borrowers have to reduce the amount of interest they pay on their mortgage — but only if it's working as intended."

However, offset accounts are often associated with higher interest rates, additional account fees or a combination of both.

Check your offset account is linked

ASIC encouraged Australians to check whether their offset account was actually set up following their initial request.

Information about offset accounts should be available via a bank's mobile app, online banking or bank statements.

Some bank sites have mortgage offset pages which outline whether a person is eligible for an offset and how to find their account number.

ASIC's report also warned that refinancing or switching home loan products could break the link between an offset account and a person's mortgage.

In just over a month, a customer paid more than $3,500 in additional interest because their offset account was not linked, ASIC found.

Tindall said: "When you've spent years building up savings in your offset, the last thing you want is for those dollars to be sitting in an account that's not actually reducing your interest bill."

"But don't stop there, do some quick maths to make sure the interest you're being charged is on the amount you actually owe, factoring in the offset balance."

What to do if something looks wrong

Customers with complaints or questions should contact their bank directly.

According to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), if a person formally raises a complaint with their bank, they must respond within 21 days for complaints involving financial difficulty or 30 days for other issues.

If a person is not satisfied with their result, they can escalate the matter to AFCA, which will act as an independent mediator at no charge.

Under the Code of Banking Practice, banks have procedures in place to deal with and resolve complaints. Source: AAP

Kathy Tannous, an economics professor at Western Sydney University, told SBS News customers can take small steps to improve their financial literacy and understanding about their offset account.

She said people should "constantly review" their home loan statements and loan repayment schedules.

"I know these days it is a lot harder because there are many branches that are closed. It's also much harder to talk to an individual because we've got lovely chatbots and so on.

"But I would say, be persistent, because the time that you're spending on this may actually save you quite a bit of money."

title: The new plan to prevent data centres from driving power prices up
text:
In brief A new plan would force data centres to invest in renewable energy.

There are fears the power-hungry data centres could cause price hikes for electricity.

Large-scale data centres will be forced to invest in additional renewable energy to fuel their operations and avoid causing power price hikes in regulations agreed to by all but two states and territories.

The Energy and Climate Change Ministerial Council revealed its plans late on Tuesday after meeting to discuss advice on the issue from the Australian Energy Market Commission.

Climate groups welcomed the announcement and boost for renewable energy, but an organisation representing data centre operators warned the policy could be counterproductive if designed without their input.

The changes come weeks after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced plans to require data centres to be powered by clean energy projects under a shake-up of artificial intelligence rules, and after a NSW data centre inquiry heard similar calls for action.

The council, which includes energy ministers from the federal government and all state and territory governments, met virtually to discuss data centre energy proposals after flagging the issue in May.

All ministers except those from Queensland and the Northern Territory agreed to pursue regulations that would "mandate that data centres offset their electricity demand by investing in additional renewable generation", the meeting communique said.

Renewable energy would need to be generated near the data centre unless local authorities opted out of the requirement, and the rules would be set at a national level, although states and territories could add additional requirements.

Changes to national rules would be considered in September, including reforms to the way data centres reported energy use.

The Climate Council called the proposed changes encouraging, although chief executive Amanda McKenzie said the rules should give data centre operators strict deadlines.

Governments from all Australian states and territories should also support the changes, she said, to avoid penalising some consumers with rising power bills.

"Unless these hold-out governments get on board, Queenslanders and Territorians will be left paying higher power bills, and we will all pay the price of higher climate pollution," she said.

But introducing a blanket rule for data centres' energy use could be ineffective if it was not designed with industry input, Data Centres Australia chief executive Belinda Dennett said.

Each centre operated differently to meet customer demands and use renewable energy, she told attendees at the Australian Clean Energy Summit, and removing options could produce poor results or deter investments.

"A one-size-fits-all approach will not work and may well be counterproductive to renewable energy investment objectives," Dennett said.

"The risk of removing this flexibility and taking a one-size-fits-all approach to energy procurement and offset arrangements may have consequences for how the data centre sector approaches renewable energy, and it's why good policy design matters and why industry needs to be at the table."

title: Where Australia sits in this $6 billion race for influence as China's strategy shifts
text:
In Brief Australia contributed the lion's share of funding to Pacific nations in need of aid in 2024, a new report has found.

China has changed its strategy from major loans to smaller, strategic forms of aid in recent years.

Australia has continued to outrank China as the Pacific's biggest source of development aid, contributing a third of loans and infrastructure investment to the region, according to a new report.

Looking at development projects across the Pacific between 2008 and 2024, the Lowy Institute report found that, after years of decline, aid to the region increased by 10 per cent in 2024.

Total development aid stood at US$4.1 billion ($5.85 billion) in that year, but the report's authors estimate that would drop to US$3.8 billion ($5.42 billion) in yet-to-be-released 2025 figures.

With China now shifting strategy from big debt-fuelled loans to smaller strategic aid, and amid major economic shocks in the Pacific, the contest for regional influence is coming under greater strain.

Australia was the Pacific's biggest donor in 2024, giving $2.14 billion in aid, which made up 37 per cent of all finance to the region in that year.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

A total of $6 billion in financing was dispensed from New Zealand, China, and regional development banks.

Australia has also inked $3.4 billion in loan deals, ending China's reign as the region's leading lender.

"That's a product of many years of Australia pushing into these spaces, but it's meant that what was once a real foothold for China in the region has been narrowed," the report's lead author Riley Duke told SBS News.

"Australia is consistently providing the most grant financing to the region, and that picture hasn't really changed."

Australia provided just over $US1.5 billion ($2.14 billion) across three sources of bilateral support to the Pacific in 2024.

The report, released on Tuesday, says demand for Chinese loans has dropped since 2019 due to concerns about servicing the debt, more competition between lenders and Chinese banks' capital availability.

Australia is also a major financier of climate change mitigation projects in the Pacific, including a solar and battery storage facility for Palau to help generate 20 per cent of its electricity, and Tonga's Renewable Energy Stabilisation Package.

The fruits of those efforts have paid off for Australia, with a flurry of regional security deals announced in recent months, including with Fiji, Vanuatu, Papua New Guinea and Tuvalu.

"They are a clear marker of Australia establishing itself as the lead partner to the region," Duke said.

"Those deals ... take a long time to progress. They're complicated, but they reflect Australia establishing itself as an inalienably important partner to Pacific countries."

Why does the Pacific rely on aid?

Developing Pacific Island nations have been hit hard by multiple shocks, including the COVID-19 pandemic and more recently, fuel supply shortages caused by the United States-Israeli war on Iran.

Duke said these multiple challenges put the region at risk of a "lost decade" of development, with Pacific economies caught in "a continual cycle of shock and recovery".

Food and importing oil costs much more for the Pacific than other countries because of transport fees, fertiliser prices and reliance on diesel generators for power.

READ MORE Australia is courting its next Pacific partner

The war on Iran is estimated to hit Pacific economic growth, shaving 1 per cent off pre-war growth projections of 3.4 per cent next year.

Australia has stepped in to help Fiji, Solomon Islands, and Samoa to help absorb fuel-price shocks and help with supply.

What is China helping build in the Pacific?

China used to be the dominant lender to the region but shifted its strategy in more recent years to focus on more "small and beautiful" projects — as President Xi Jinping has described it — to win regional influence.

"China's lending collapse to the region, sort of meant that it had to pivot or adapt how it engaged through aid and development channels, and how that's materialised is these smaller, more grassroots projects," Duke said.

"China is offering more training. It's been donating more equipment, more scholarships, and you know it's trying to find new ways to build relationships with Pacific countries."

Those smaller donations include equipment to schools, police forces, and hospitals across the Pacific, as well as training to build up regional health, media, and policing industries.

Its largest single grant is a US$135 million ($192.63 million) project for new roads and bridges in Fiji, followed by the Nauru National Sports Stadium (US$73 million), the Vanuatu Earthquake Recovery Grant (US $57 million), and the High School Sports Complex in Tonga (US$26 million).

Duke said Chinese aid in the Pacific is "highly reactive" to diplomatic developments, and acts as a "strategic lever".

"When a country switches diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing, or opens strategic negotiations with Australia, Chinese aid flows react."

One example is Nauru's 2024 switch of diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing — after which a flurry of Chinese aid followed, including the stadium project.

The report also found Chinese state-owned firms dominate contracts for infrastructure projects, including for multilateral projects.

title: 'Hidden harm': The $17k offset account failure that exposes banks' costly blind spot
text:
IN BRIEF A report by ASIC has found that some banks failed to deliver promises on offset account savings.

The Australian Banking Association said banks take any identified issues very seriously and have compensated customers impacted.

Offset accounts are often marketed as a simple way to reduce home loan interest, but a report by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) has found that some banks fail to deliver on that promise.

ASIC, Australia's financial services and consumer credit regulator, reviewed the offset practices of eight banks, which together represent more than 70 per cent of Australia's approximately $2.5 trillion home loan market.

It found that, while practices varied across these financial institutions — AMP, ANZ, CommBank, Great Southern Bank, HSBC Australia, ING, Macquarie Bank and Westpac — there were weaknesses in how they established, monitored and managed offset accounts.

It identified two cases where customers unknowingly paid more than $17,000 extra interest on their home loan because the bank did not make clear that offset accounts had to be re-linked after refinancing.

In another circumstance, a customer paid over $3,500 in additional interest over about a month after their account was incorrectly de-linked.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Reports to ASIC between 1 September 2023 and 31 August 2025 showed banks paid more than $55 million in customer compensation for offset account failures.

It expects compensation to continue as banks further analyse offset account operations.

ASIC chair Sarah Court said that "when offset accounts don't operate correctly, the harm can be hidden".

"Loan repayments stay the same, while customers unknowingly pay more interest and take longer to repay their loan."

What is an offset account?

Hue Hwa Au Yong, a senior lecturer in banking and finance at Monash University, said offset accounts are "simple to understand but difficult for customers to verify".

Like an everyday transaction account, offset accounts can be used to deposit and withdraw money.

However, the amount of money in an offset account also reduces the outstanding amount owed on a home loan, which is used to calculate interest.

If a person has $50,000 in their offset account and a $750,000 loan, they will only be charged interest on $700,000.

"So, the issue really is not the product itself, but the system behind it," Yong told SBS News.

"As a bank customer, we can see how much money is in our offset account. But as a borrower, we can't easily verify whether the banking systems are correctly applying it when calculating interest, [which] ... is calculated daily using a quite complex formula and system. "

Australian Banking Association CEO Simon Birmingham told SBS News that offset accounts "can be an effective way for mortgage holders to save on interest and in more than 99 per cent of cases banks were found to manage them correctly".

He said banks had "already taken action to compensate the small number of customers where those banks identified errors, often manual errors".

Offset accounts in Australia

As of March this year, Australians had almost $350 billion in offset accounts, a 28 per cent increase over the past two years, according to ASIC.

Kathy Tannous — a professor in economics at Western Sydney University's Business School — said offset accounts are becoming increasingly popular.

"Around 40 per cent of all mortgage holders use an offset account according to recent research," Tannous told SBS News.

"Part of the appeal is twofold in Australia: our level of housing ownership but also the size of our mortgages — the amount we have to borrow relative to our income in order to buy what we call the 'Australian dream' of owning a property".

Offset accounts are an increasingly popular option for many mortgage holders in Australia. Source: Getty / Ingrid_Hendriksen

However, offset accounts are also associated with higher interest rates, additional account fees or a combination of both.

Offset accounts are not available in the United States due to tax regulations. They are an option in New Zealand and the United Kingdom, but are less common than in Australia.

Customers 'doubly hit'

According to ASIC's report, there are several key reasons why banks have "insufficient oversight and inadequate responses" to customers regarding offset accounts.

The regulator found some banks "struggled" to readily identify if or when customers had requested an offset account.

It also alleged banks were unaware they were failing to deliver on promises for offset accounts.

It claims some financial institutions were slow to fix issues, compensate customers and didn't provide easily accessible online information.

Court said that, when offset account failures occur, "customers are doubly hit" — not only losing promised interest savings but also the opportunity to use that money elsewhere.

The report also provides examples of "more positive action by banks", including improvements to offset practices before and during the review.

Some banks have committed to make changes after ASIC's reporting, according to the regulator.

Calls for change?

Tannous believes in Australia, some people rely on banks, "almost like you're relying on your doctor to treat you medically".

"You rely on banks to treat you financially. That they will provide you with information in a way that you can understand it and make a decision."

She described ASIC's report as "most concerning" but acknowledged the regulator's findings were limited to a two-year period.

ASIC has called for greater transparency from banks to amend what it has described as weaknesses in offset account practices. That includes information about offset accounts on bank websites and mobile apps.

Yong said the onus should be on banks, not customers, to detect errors in offset accounts but also encouraged Australians to be "proactive" and contact their bank if they had concerns.

Birmingham also said "banks take any identified issues very seriously, with these banks already compensating their customers and taking steps to further strengthen their offset account practices".

title: Gina Rinehart funded flights and fashion show for Pauline Hanson

title: Australia has a favourite day to say 'I do' — but fewer couples are saying it
text:
In brief New Australian Bureau of Statistics data reveals 25 October was the most popular wedding date last year.

It also found the marriage rate continued to decline, and the divorce rate ticked up for the first time in years.

Saturday 25 October was Australia's favourite day to say "I do" in 2025 — but new data suggests fewer couples are saying it.

Fewer Australians tied the knot last year than the year before, according to new figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

At the same time, more marriages are coming to an end, with the divorce rate ticking upward for the first time in several years, though ultimately remaining lower than it was 20 years ago.

The most popular day to get hitched

The most popular wedding date in 2025 was Saturday 25 October — i.e. the symmetrical 25/10/25 — with 2,035 marriages.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

That's about 500 more than the runner-up, Saturday 22 November (22/11/25) — which had 1,527.

ABS data show there's somewhat of a trend towards more marriages on dates with numerical significance, though for some it could also be coincidence.

The least popular days were Christmas Day, with 51 weddings, Boxing Day with 54, New Year's Day with 57, and Tuesday 29 July with 61.

Spring dominated the wedding calendar, with most of the top ten dates falling in September, October and November. The rest were scattered across autumn.

Last year, 25/10/25 was the most popular date for Australians to tie the knot. Source: SBS News

Saturday remains, unsurprisingly, the nation's preferred wedding day — more than 52,000 marriages took place on a Saturday in 2025, and 45 of the year's most popular dates fell on one.

Friday came in second, with just over 21,000 marriages, led by Friday 10 October (10/10/25).

Zoom out further, and one day still reigns supreme: 10 November 2012 — the sequential 10/11/12.

That remains the most popular wedding date of the past 20 years, with 3,081 marriages recorded on that day — still comfortably ahead of the runner-up, 11 November 2011 (11/11/11), which had 2,614.

Fewer couples tying the knot

Beyond the calendar quirks, the broader numbers tell a clearer story: marriage is becoming less common in Australia.

There were 118,804 marriages registered in 2025 — 2,040 fewer than in 2024, a drop of 1.7 per cent.

That's in line with 2023's total (118,439), but still well above the pandemic-era lows of 2020 and 2021.

Adjusted for population, the marriage rate — the number of marriages per 1,000 people aged 16 and over — fell slightly to 5.3 in 2025, down from 5.5 in both 2023 and 2024.

Zoom out to 2005, where the marriage rate was 6.9, and the decline is even more stark.

The biggest drops came among 25-29 and 30-34 year-olds. No age group recorded an increase.

In the last 20 years, Australia's marriage rate has declined — but so has the proportion of people getting divorced. Source: SBS News

Despite the falling numbers, the age at which Australians marry has barely moved: 32.7 years for men (down marginally from 32.8 in 2024) and 31.2 years for women, unchanged for the third year running.

Same-sex and non-binary marriages held steady too, making up 3.9 per cent of all marriages for a third consecutive year. More marriages were between two women (2,527) than two men (1,849).

More couples calling it quits

On the other side of the ledger, 49,158 divorces were granted in 2025, a 4.1 per cent rise on 2024's 47,216.

That brings the total roughly back in line with 2022 levels (49,241).

The divorce rate — divorces per 1,000 people aged 16 and over — rose to 2.2, up from 2.1 in 2024.

But the bigger picture across two decades reveals fewer people are getting divorced: in 2005, the divorce rate was 3.3 per 1,000 people, compared to 2025's 2.2 figure.

READ MORE Kate says her cancer led to divorce. The aftermath of it was even more surprising

Australians are also divorcing slightly later in life: the median age at divorce rose to 47.3 years for men and 44.4 for women, both up marginally on 2024.

But marriages that do end are lasting longer before couples separate — a median of 9.4 years in 2025, up from 9.3 the year before.

That data suggests Australians may be walking down the aisle less often each year, but marriages may be proving more durable than they were two decades ago.

title: Origin apologises after revealing 900,000 customers affected by data breach
text:
In Brief Origin says 900,000 customers were affected by a data breach.

It's advising customers to be wary of a heightened risk of scammers.

Almost one million Origin Energy customers had their details accessed by hackers after a major data breach last week, the company has revealed.

On Tuesday, Origin said it had completed an initial review into the incident and identified that approximately 900,000 current and former customers' data was accessed by the hackers.

"To our customers, I am sorry. We don't take for granted the trust customers place in Origin and our safeguarding of their information," CEO Frank Calabria said in a statement.

Last week, the energy company announced it was the victim of the security incident, saying names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers and account information could all have been viewed.

Other potential details include the last four digits of credit cards, or the last three digits of bank accounts.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The company said it would be contacting affected customers first and was opening up a dedicated hotline for those concerned.

Origin said it had been trying to confirm the credibility of the threat since early July.

"We worked to confirm its credibility and potential impact; however, based on the information available, it was not assessed to be credible," Calabria said.

READ MORE Origin Energy reports customer bank, credit card details caught up in data breach

"On 22 July, new information emerged that indicated a potential security incident may have occurred. We acted immediately, providing updates to the market and notifying our customers as a precaution."

Origin, which has 4.8 million customer accounts in Australia and provides electricity, natural gas, LPG and internet services, said last week it did not believe the data obtained included credit card or bank details.

Customers advised to be wary of scams

The company has also warned customers to be alert to a greater risk of scams that could arise from the data breach, advising customers to be wary of unexpected calls, emails or texts referring to their account.

Those who get such contact should independently contact Origin through numbers on official channels, it said, and do not provide passwords or personal information to anyone.

"We are acutely aware that others may exploit this incident, including by impersonating Origin or through other scam activity," Calabria said.

"We recommend that all our customers remain vigilant to suspicious activity and a heightened risk of scams.

Griffith University's Graeme Hughes, an expert on business and consumer issues, said the breach was unlikely to cause cases of payment fraud but marked a "social engineering problem".

"The last four digits for a card, a date of birth, and an authentic billing history are the exact trust signals a business uses to verify itself over the phone," Hughes told the Australian Associated Press.

"That makes an unsolicited call about an energy account far more convincing than it should be.

title: 'I'm not Jacinta Allan': Caroll pledges 'new direction' and calls a royal commission
text:
In Brief Jacinta Allan announced her resignation shortly before a party room meeting that would have seen a leadership spill.

Deputy Premier Ben Carroll was elected to the tob job after a lengthy, chaotic meeting.

New Victorian Premier Ben Carroll has declared he will lead his government in a "new direction", while distancing himself from his predecessors Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews.

In his first comments after being elected state Labor leader, Carroll also announced a royal commission into the construction sector, which has been marred by corruption allegations, and the strengthening of Victoria's anti-corruption watchdog.

Allan had consistently rejected calls for an inquiry.

"Let me make one thing very clear: I am not Daniel Andrews. I am not Jacinta Allan," he said on Tuesday afternoon, just hours after Allan's resignation.

"I will do things differently, because different times require a new approach.
